subtopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING EXTENDED SITTINGS

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Secretary of Stale):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING EXTENDED SITTINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might be permitted, before you call the motion standing in my name, to say a brief word about the business of the house. It might be that we would not necessarily deal with the motion after I have said this.
I think all hon. members are aware that the motion was put on the order paper because of the difficult situation in which the country finds itself at the present time. The government realizes that it is an inconvenience with as short notice as this to ask hon. members to sit on Saturday, but I would like to be allowed to remind hon. members that we are in a rather difficult position, particularly with respect to supply. Perhaps it is not altogether realized in the house that ten days of this session will have to be taken up- unless they are foregone and there is no suggestion they should be-with supply motions; and in view of the fact that only one department has been disposed of and another not completely disposed of, I do not think, bearing in mind past practice, that we could reasonably anticipate much less than 20 days on estimates, which makes 30 sitting days.
If we are to get this session finished by the end of the year, which I am sure all hon. members would like to do, this is a fact of life, in addition to which there is some
difficult and contentious legislation and some legislation that may not be contentious but still is important and deserves to be seriously debated. This is a problem not just for the government; this is a problem for the whole house.
It had been my thought that perhaps the most satisfactory way of dealing with it would be to have a motion adopted which would give us the power to sit on Saturdays whenever it seemed necessary in order to make progress on the estimates, but I am not going to ask the house to do that without proper notice. We have a very important bill before us which the government and all hon. members have indicated they feel should be disposed of, and we have two other matters that are important in the sense that the elections in the Northwest Territories will be governed by them. But I am wondering whether it might be possible to avoid putting this motion at all provided there was some other way by which hon. members thought adequate progress could be made today. Since I have not had the opportunity for the usual consultations I thought I might put the matter to the house and see whether we might be able to resolve it without the necessity of my moving the motion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING EXTENDED SITTINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the difficulties that face the house with regard to the organization of business are pretty well known to hon. members, and what the Secretary of State has said with regard to the estimates is quite correct. We have quite a problem to deal with the estimates. In a year when an election is held it is just inevitable that in that calendar year there is a restricted time for estimates. I made a survey last year and compared four election years. That survey showed clearly that the house either has to shorten the period for the study of estimates or not pass the estimates completely at all.
We are now in that position in this calendar year. The house has to make a decision whether we will telescope the time for estimates or whether we will drift on and not pass them all. I am not going to stir up any political discussion as to what was done last year or anything of that nature, but this is the situation that faces the House of Commons in a year in which an election is held.
I suggest that this particular motion stand so that we will have a little time to consult together and propose various plans for the

Business of the House allocation of time during the balance of the calendar year. It may be that we can work out something that will be satisfactory.
In so far as today is concerned, if the debate on the bill which is to be the first item of business to come before us is not prolonged, I presume it would then be possible to go on with the other two bills that have been mentioned. I have not had time to consult with the members of our party, but my own preference would be to sit a bit longer today rather than to sit on Saturday. Second, even if we feel that Saturday sittings are necessary I would prefer that consideration of this matter be postponed and that Saturday sittings, if we have to have them, come later in this calendar year.
In conclusion may I just say that I think it would be agreeable to us to sit longer hours today if necessary, rather than reassembling tomorrow.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING EXTENDED SITTINGS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we recognize the problem that faces the house at the present time, and are quite prepared to co-operate in every reasonable effort to get the business of the house through. We know it is absolutely necessary that adequate time be given to the departmental estimates because this gives individual members an opportunity to deal with their respective problems. We have not had an opportunity of discussing this in our party either, but I believe the suggestion that has been made, that we sit tonight even up to ten o'clock if necessary, will be satisfactory; and it might be preferable in the circumstances rather than sitting tomorrow.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING EXTENDED SITTINGS

Mr. Speaker, I think the Secretary of State is to be be commended for his suggestion that we not proceed with his motion at the moment but that we be given time to consider the points he has raised. We are all aware of the problem facing us with respect to getting the estimates through, and I think we would all admit that we have to find some way in which we can do this in the amount of time there is left in the calendar year before another session starts.
I would suggest that the question of whether we sit tonight or tomorrow for the purpose of getting the trusteeship legislation through, as well as the whole question of what to do about our sittings, be discussed through what are sometimes referred to as the usual channels but which seem to have broken down a bit of late. I am suggesting to the Secretary of State that he resume the very commendable practice he carried on in the early part of the session, of calling in the house leaders of the various parties to discuss these matters. I know the problem this raises, but I suggest


that common sense dictates that if we are going to deal with the business of the house, a representative of every group in the house, by whatever name it is called, should meet with the Secretary of State to work this out.
I think if we do have such a meeting today we can can come up with some solution to the problem. I urge that nothing be done at this point, but that the representatives of the various groups have a chance to discuss the matter with the members of their parties and that the Secretary of State call a meeting of the party representatives later this day.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING EXTENDED SITTINGS
speechtext: I suggest to the house that as a matter of courtesy, and shall we say fair play, certainly without prejudice to any statement made by me, we do hear this morning from the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire).

speechtext:
Surely, Mr. Speaker, it is important, in order to speed up the business of the house, to have the opinion of a political party which includes 13 members.
It would be easier to co-ordinate the business if our group of 13 members is consulted than otherwise. As far as we are concerned, we think it is normal that these things be discussed among the parliamentary leaders in order to reach a solution, so that the business of the house be accelerated as much as possible.
From what I understood of the statement made by the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickers-gill), he is anxious to see the trusteeship bill pass today or tomorrow and we have no objection to that. On the other hand, as far as Bills C-83 and C-84 are concerned, even if there are agreements between the parliamentary leaders of the various parties, we wish to point out that we would not want to put a blockade on the passing of those bills but that we think we are dealing with very important legislation, particularly the bill respecting the delimitation of the Nunassiaq territory and that we could not accept, at least under the present circumstances, a speedy consideration of that bill in as much as it is lacking in precision and clearness and it does not contain the full information we would like to have. Besides, we just pointed out that fact to the leader of the house and that, without any intention of filibustering. But those questions are very important to us and we want to consider them. Therefore, and as was done in the past, we suggest a meeting between the parliamentary leaders of the various political parties including ours, to discuss the situation of the business of the house at the present time.

subtopic: STATEMENT BY SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING EXTENDED SITTINGS
speechtext:
I should like to deal first of all with one point raised by the hon. member for Lapointe. Let me say at once that this government has no intention of seeking to put through any piece of legislation without allowing hon. members who want to debate any point of principle to do so. There is no thought whatever of suggesting that if there is any intention of debating the substance of this bill, that will be a condition of anything else; because that is what parliament is for, to debate these matters. There will be no attempt on the part of the government to push this bill through until hon. members are satisfied that they have had their say before the matter is brought to a vote. I am referring to the bill in connection with the territory the name of which, because of my poor knowledge of Eskimo, I cannot pronounce.
As to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I think it would be satisfactory to the government if we could reach an agreement now that it would be possible at five o'clock to revert to motions to settle this question for the rest of the week. Speaking as house leader and also for the government, we in other words, do not want to be denied the right which we now have to move our motion; but if it could be agreed now that, in the event of our not being able to find any satisfactory solution, we could revert to motions at five o'clock and have freedom to deal with the matter, I think it would be very helpful; and it would save the time of the house if we could have discussions through the usual channels about this matter.
I should like to say at the same time that I appreciate very much indeed the co-operative and understanding way in which this matter has been approached by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre and indeed by all those who have spoken. If we could have this understanding that the house would permit us to revert to motions to adopt whatever procedure may be agreed upon or, in the event of no agreement, that the government may go ahead, should it still feel it is necessary to do so, with the motion, I think this matter could be postponed for the time being.

maintopic: WHEAT-STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING MARKETING POLICY

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: WHEAT-STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING MARKETING POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will recall that yesterday I endeavoured to make a rather lengthy reply to some questions which were put to me about Canadian-United States wheat marketing policies, and it was suggested that I might instead make the statement today on motions, which I am very happy to do.
I said in the course of my reply to an hon. member that Canada and the United States are competitors in world wheat markets, friendly competitors but very keen competitors. I said that we were each interested in getting as large a share of world markets as we could, and also that we had a very great interest in stability. That is why we are both members of the international wheat agreement, and it is why we have had from time to time consultations about our respective wheat policies. I recalled that when the joint committee on trade and economic affairs was established some years ago a subcommittee was established at the official level just for the purpose of discussing our respective wheat policies, and in particular at that time surplus disposal, which has been carried on in the United States over the years on a very large scale. I also said there were many times when our two governments have not always seen eye to eye, when we have made representations the one to the other.
This is natural and normal, since we remain competitors, even though, like wheat importing and exporting countries generally, we have an interest as members of the international wheat agreement in the stabilization of the world wheat market.
The wheat marketing systems of Canada and the United States are, of course, very different. In Canada the Canadian wheat board is the sole marketing agency for western wheat. The wheat board sells the wheat at home and abroad and distributes the proceeds to the farmers. No one stands between the farmer and the export market.
In the United States, on the other hand, the domestic market price has been above the price of wheat being offered by competitive sellers like Canada, Australia and

Wheat Marketing Policy the Argentine. In order to meet this competition the United States government has had to pay a subsidy fixed from time to time. In addition, as hon. members know, the United States government has moved very large quantities of wheat under the provisions of public law 480.
The Canadian wheat board, being the sole marketing agency for western wheat, determines its selling prices from day to day, and may enter into contracts of any size and for forward delivery. This it did recently for
500,000	tons to mainland China and nearly six million tons of wheat and flour to the Soviet union.
After the conclusion of the Russian contract the board indicated its willingness to enter into forward contracts also with certain of its regular customers, including Japanese buyers. It seems to me this was a sensible and forward looking policy, since the board is desirous of retaining the business and the good will of its regular customers.
The United States administration has taken exception to this policy and has let its views be known to the press, as well as to the Canadian wheat board and to the government. All I can say is that I believe the wheat board has been acting in the long term interests of the western farmer, and in a way designed to promote stability in world wheat markets. If, over the years and recently, it had followed a less far seeing policy, I do not believe those in need of wheat would have turned as they did to Canada in the first instance for such a large portion of their requirements.
I am sure all hon. members on all sides of the house will agree that it is of the utmost importance that the wheat board should take the long view. Even with these large sales Canada will still have a large carryover at the end of the current crop year. We intend to remain competitive, to retain our regular customers and their confidence in our marketing system, and to build new markets.
I trust we shall also continue to have the co-operation of the United States administration in doing what can be done to stabilize world wheat markets.

maintopic: WHEAT-STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING MARKETING POLICY
speechtext:
I hope the house has followed with interest and deep attention the remarks which have been made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. What the hon. gentleman has said about the marketing of grain was accurate and succinct. It was not altogether complete, of course, and the suggestions I am about to make will, I trust, add weight to what has been said.
We have been operating in Canada, through the Canadian wheat board, a type of marketing which I think ranks with the best in any


country in the world. Because of lack of knowledge on the part of many people in Canada, some of them in high places, about the way in which the wheat board operates, attacks are occasionally made on the board for which there can be no justifiable foundation.
The matters which are now under discussion were, of course, considered at the time we set the policy in connection with the China wheat agreement. In connection with this long term agreement we held to the view that we could set a fixed price for the period of each contract. This fixed price basis has been followed by the board as a regular policy, without any objection being raised until the present time. The minister was correct when he pointed out that this was the established practice of the wheat board, with the full knowledge of our competitors.
The second point I wish to make is that we have established what I call a rule of law in the sale of grain on world markets. We have set an example to nations which produce surpluses of other types as to the way in which they can bring a rule of law into the marketing of their products. Until the last two or three weeks I was very proud of the co-operation which existed among the leading exporting nations of the world in dealing with their customers, passing information back and forth and maintaining the confidence of each.
During the last two weeks it looked as if we were reaching the breaking point in the confidence that we must have if our Canadian wheat board officials are to divulge all our Canadian information to our competitors as they divulge their information to us. I would hope that the minister, at his level, would bring to the attention of his United States counterpart the fact that we want to maintain this friendly co-operation and rule of law in connection with the handling of grain in the world through this international wheat agreement. We would hope that he would restrain his officials, and if necessary himself, from making statements which are harmful to the interests of one of the countries co-operating in this group. I do not believe we should allow our officials to stand alone on this question. I think if you do it over the telephone you can make it very clear to the secretary of agriculture that these are views which, as Canadians, we all support, and that we support the Canadian wheat board.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that we would like to support him in his determination to maintain the selling procedures that the Canadian wheat board has followed in the past. I should like to say to him also that we feel it is both right and desirable that the wheat board

ditions and terms equally favourable as they gave in the special sales to mainland China and the Soviet union. If these forward pricing arrangements had been carried on in the past, and the minister tells us they had, then we support him in his contention that they should be continued in spite of objection from the United States.

maintopic: WHEAT-STATEMENT BY MINISTER RESPECTING MARKETING POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the events of the past few years in relation to the marketing of wheat have fully vindicated the establishment of the Canadian wheat board as the sole marketing agency of wheat and certain coarse grains in this country. The huge surpluses which had been built up would have resulted, under an open market situation, in very depressed prices for the farmers. Now the shortage of wheat in certain areas of the world would have resulted in a very rapid increase in the world price which would have benefited not the farmers who grew the wheat but the speculators on the various wheat exchanges. Therefore the organization of a national wheat marketing policy has been fully vindicated by the present situation, in that the farmer is going to get the full return from whatever wheat is sold and the purchasers of wheat, who are important, are not going to feel that they have been exploited because of an unfortunate famine situation.
This does not mean, of course, that we think the Canadian wheat board should drop its price in order to get orders. It was for this reason I was concerned when the report came from Washington that the Canadian wheat board had dropped its price 6 cents a bushel in order to get a contract with mainland China. However, I believe we have to leave it to the good judgment of the Canadian wheat board to get the best price they can.
I was relieved yesterday when the minister denied the statement which was made by a United States agriculture spokesman to the effect that on September 20 a representative from Canada had assured the United States representative that no more fixed price agreements would be entered into following the agreement with the Soviet union. I am glad the minister has assured the house and the country that such fixed price agreements will be continued, because they are in the interests of the farmer on the one hand, and fully demonstrate to importers of wheat that we are not anxious to allow speculators to take advantage of the unfortunate situation which has made it necessary for them tc import large quantities of wheat.
I think the house generally will support the minister in the position which he has
Wheat Marketing Policy taken, and will let the Canadian wheat board know that we stand behind the policy they have been pursuing.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harry W. Hays (Minister of Agriculture):
maintopic: BUTTER-STATEMENT ON SALE OF SURPLUS STOCKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,	since I	have	hadmany inquiries in connection with the butter situation	I thought I	should review	thesituation	at this time	for the	benefit of
hon. members.
As one of the supports provided to the dairy industry under the Agricultural Stabilization Act, butter has been supported by an offer to purchase. In 1957 the level of support	was increased	from 58	cents	per
pound to 64 cents per pound. Until that time production and consumption of butter in Canada had remained reasonably in balance. In 1958, with the increase in the support level and concurrent anti-fat publicity, the per capita consumption dropped sharply while production continued to rise. By May 1, 1962 the agricultural stabilization board's stocks of butter either as butter or in the form of butter oil had risen to 168 million pounds. Of this over 70 million pounds had been accumulated during the 1961-62 support year.
On May 1, 1962 a consumption incentive program of 12 cents per pound was instituted, and during that year approximately 50 million pounds more butter was moved into domestic disappearance channels than was the case the previous year. Nevertheless, production for the dairy year 1962-63 exceeded consumption by approximately 25 million pounds. At the start of this dairy year certain changes were made in the support program, including a modest incentive to the production of Cheddar cheese, a product that finds ready acceptance in the export market. As a consequence of this and the continuation of the 12 cent consumption subsidy it appears that this year for the first time since 1957 supply and demand of dairy products will be approximately in balance.
In order to reduce storage costs and to conserve quality, older stocks of butter from time to time have been converted to butter oil. While Canada to date has refrained from offering surplus butter on the world market at concessional prices, the fact that the current program now would appear to have the surplus problem under control would indicate that it is appropriate to dispose of at least a portion of the holdings of surplus butter and butter oil. Crop conditions throughout parts of Europe and Asia have been unsatisfactory this year, which would indicate an over-all shortage of dairy products. Accordingly after consultation with major dairy exporting countries the government decided to offer for 
export the agricultural stabilization board's holdings of butter oil.
Early this week word was received that Great Britain needed supplies of butter to meet imminent shortages which could not be covered because of distance, supply conditions and seasonal factors by Great Britain's normal suppliers. Accordingly the British board of trade asked British importers to submit applications for the import, from any source, of 5,000 tons of butter for delivery prior to November 15. The agricultural stabilization board quoted 1961 and 1962 butter at competitive prices to Canadian exporters who had received inquiries from British importers. To date it is understood that approximately one half of the import licences are being issued to cover butter from Canadian sources.
It is not considered to be in the interests of the competitive position of Canadian exporters to release the price at which the agricultural stabilization board has quoted this butter at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Prime Minister in connection with the statements made yesterday by United States secretary of labour Wirtz, which apparently reflect the opinions of the Kennedy administration on the measure before the Canadian parliament to set up a maritime unions trusteeship.
Has the Prime Minister, either on the hot line between Washington and Ottawa or through the ordinary facilities, advised President Kennedy personally of the indignation of Canadians at the unwarranted affront to the parliament of Canada and the people of Canada by the observations of a man holding

the responsible post that Mr. Wirtz does, regarding measures before our parliament and while they are being discussed here?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MARITIME UNIONS TRUSTEESHIP
subsubtopic: STATEMENTS BY U.S. OFFICIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to answer the right hon. gentleman's statement and question at some length and crave the indulgence of the house for that purpose, but I might say at the beginning that I have not communicated directly with President Kennedy on this particular matter, as the full account of the statements that were made in Washington yesterday were received only this morning. I refer to the statements made by the secretary of labour and the president of the American federation of labour, statements that were carried in yesterday's press reports.
The Minister of Labour and other hon. members of the house have already expressed their deep concern over both the content and the timing of these statements. The concern that I am sure members of the house and Canadians generally have felt about these statements arises in large part from the apparent failure of both the secretary of labour of the United States government and the president of the A.F.L.-C.I.O. to appreciate fully the fact that the dispute on the great lakes is essentially a Canadian dispute, although of course it has international ramifications and could cause international repercussions.
In all the efforts that have been made to develop an effective solution to this problem on a private basis the failure on the part of the United States labour leaders to recognize this basic fact, that this was basically a Canadian dispute, has been a chief stumbling block. For instance, the insistence of the A.F.L.-C.I.O. negotiators that there should be no provision in any private trusteeship arrangement to ensure that the majority of the trustees be Canadian was indeed a major issue on which private negotiations broke down. The government let the Canadian Labour Congress spokesmen know from the beginning of the negotiations that it strongly supported the stand taken by the congress on this matter, and that the government could accept no private arrangement that did not ensure a Canadian majority of trustees. Any other course would have been unthinkable, and it is surprising that the United States government and labour officials did not realize this.
Another basic fact that has not been recognized in the Washington statements is the failure once again on their part to understand that this dispute-and I have already referred to this-centres around the progressive destruction of free trade unionism and the failure of the president of the seafarers international union of Canada to arrest this progressive destruction of democratic unioninquiries of the Ministry ism. The objective of the government, and I am sure of the parliament of Canada, of the Canadian Labour Congress and of the Canadian people, is to restore free and democratic unionism in the maritime industry in Canada, and complete freedom of shipping on the great lakes. That is the essence of our position and explains the reason that the Canadian parliament is being asked to do what the S.I.U. itself should have done long ago.
I would hope especially that the statement made by Mr. Meany, rightly described by my friend the Minister of Labour as shocking, is not to be interpreted as an invitation to violence on the part of members of unions. The Canadian government and the Canadian people will not, I can assure Mr. Meany if he needs the assurance, be intimidated let alone impressed by any such statements.

subtopic: MARITIME TRANSPORTATION UNIONS

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour) moved
subtopic: MARITIME TRANSPORTATION UNIONS
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-102, to provide for the placing of the maritime transportation unions of Canada under the management and control of trustees.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving the second reading of this bill I point out that it is clear to hon. members that the principle of the bill is to place the maritime transportation unions in Canada under the management and control of trustees. The bill is now before hon. members of the house, and my purpose at this stage is to comment on the bill in more detail than was possible at the resolution stage.
Members of the house, in considering the bill, should be reminded that the trusteeship will cover five maritime labour organizations. These organizations are set forth in schedule B on the last page of the bill. The membership of these unions is as follows: first, the Canadian maritime union, consisting of one local with 500 members; second, the seafarers international union of Canada, with two divisions and consisting of 17,400 members; third, the national association of marine engineers of Canada, with seven locals and 150 members; fourth, the Canadian merchant service guild, with two divisions and 2,480 members; and finally the Canadian brotherhood of railway, transport and general workers, consisting of 13 locals with a membership of 2,297 persons.
Members of the house are also aware that each of the five organizations has its own constitution and a number of collective labour agreements. For that reason it is abundantly clear that none of us should be thinking of trusteeship legislation as applying solely to one organization.
I would like to emphasize that the normal principles of free and democratic labour organizations and the normal employer-employee relationship through collective labour agreements are emphasized in the legislation. It should be clear that the trustees are asked in and empowered by the legislation to manage and control each of the maritime unions; but they are also asked to do all things necessary or advisable for the return of the management and control of each of the maritime unions to duly elected and responsible officers of such unions at the earliest date consistent with the national and public interest of Canada.
In making that statement, Mr. Speaker, I want to underline my view that certainly all the locals and all the unions that are placed under this trusteeship are not being placed in the same category as the particular union

which gave rise to this legislation. I want to make it clear that the officers of certain unions have agreed to come under this trusteeship willingly in the interests of cleaning up the situation on the great lakes, and their inclusion in this legislation is certainly not intended to imply that the strictures contained in the Norris commission report which apply to the seafarers international union of Canada apply in any way whatsoever to the other unions involved. I think it ought to be made clear that the inclusion has been voluntarily on the part of these unions in the interests of unionism and in the national interest.
The trustees are to carry out this principle of restoring the management and control of the maritime unions to duly elected and responsible officers. The trustees will be empowered to establish advisory councils, to recommend changes in the constitution or bylaws of the unions, to supervise and tender advice to bargaining committees in the negotiating of collective labour agreements, and to carry out the normal management and control of union affairs. The intention of the legislation, and it has been prepared with this intention in mind, is that the trustees will, in so far as it is possible, administer the operations of the unions referred to as nearly as possible in accord with properly and democratically operated labour organizations.
Having said that, it is also clear that the trustees will be asked to undertake a very heavy responsibility, and they will be asked to resolve a very serious and critical situation. For that reason they will have power and authority to deal with any situation that may arise and with which they may be confronted. This power and authority is provided in the legislation. This authority of the trustees is further strengthened by penalty provisions against any obstruction of the trustees or any withholding of documents and information that may be required by them. It is a natural course of events that as well as supervising the employer-employee relationship, the investments of union members in their respective organizations must be protected. This is also provided for in the legislation. Members of the house will have noticed that reference is made to a building corporation, and provision is made for the trustees to exercise management and control of this corporation.
Hon. members will appreciate that it is difficult to know fully what may have transpired within any union since the date of the report of Mr. Justice Norris. For this reason there is provision in the bill for a preserving status. There is provision empowering the trustees to apply for a court
Maritime Transportation Unions
order to declare void any transaction entered into on or after the 6th day of July, 1963, pursuant to certain provisions which are spelled out in the legislation. Similar authority is given to the trustees in another part of the bill. In other words it is desirable that a status quo should have prevailed since the receipt of the report of Mr. Justice Norris. In addition, provision is made that an annual report is to be made to the Minister of Labour by the trustees, and that report shall be laid before parliament.
Naturally members of the house will want to examine carefully each detail of the legislation so as to ensure that the purposes of the trustees will be carried out, that the legislation will be effective, and that the trustees will be able to operate effectively. There has been some question about why this legislation continues for a period of five years. Naturally it is hoped that it will not continue for this period of time. I assure hon. members that consideration was given to providing for a shorter period. As hon. members will notice from the legislation, every possible provision is included to permit the removal of any maritime union from the trusteeship at an earlier date. It may be quite possible that all the trustees named in the legislation will have been removed from the trusteeship before December 31, 1968.
Having made that comment, I should like to say that we are undertaking a very serious task. We ought it seems to me, to avoid two extremes. One is to make the period of trusteeship so short that it may encourage a restoration of conditions which prevail at the present time in any of the unions; that it may encourage any person to wait out this trusteeship in an effort to once again wrest control over any union for his own purposes. On the other hand, there is a natural reluctance on the part of members of parliament to give these powers to trustees for a day longer than is absolutely necessary.
I have not a closed mind on this point, and neither has the government. All I am concerned with is that the trusteeship be effective. I hope there will be very careful consideration given to maintaining the effectiveness of the trusteeship, and I would not want it to become ineffective in its purposes through having too short a period available to enable the trusteeship to work properly.
In conclusion, both on second reading of the bill and when we go into committee I will consider any further views on this matter, and I hope it will be possible in committee to reach a meeting of minds on this very important point.

subtopic: MARITIME TRANSPORTATION UNIONS
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on this question at the resolution stage was featured by a certain

Maritime Transportation Unions amount of recrimination, but the fact is that almost anyone can share some of the blame for the existence of the situation created by Mr. Banks. Certainly it is easy to point the finger at a former government-I say government, not governments-and at trade union leaders in Canada. There are some very deep questions to be asked about the behaviour of the management of certain companies in all these dealings, and in this sense I do not think anyone can take a great deal of pride in the efforts we are now making to clean up the situation. I do not want to go into recriminations again; I just want to speak for my party and not for anyone else, but I presume that along tha way other people will speak as Canadian nationalists with regard to this whole matter.
I have had some dealings with the S.I.U., since it happens to have a branch in my constituency. Members of my party organization belong to the S.I.U., and I have had quite a bit of contact with them. I know that this measure may cause trouble in my own area owing to the fact that the port council, which consists of a number of unions, do associate with the S.I.U., and the longshoremen are likely to take some steps. The repercussions at the local level are obvious to me and other members who have to deal with the S.I.U. Already we have had evidence today of the repercussions at the international level. It seems to me that we need a fundamental unity in our approach to this matter, which I suggest should be an approach based on Canadian nationalism.
When I say that I do not mean that we should contradict any of the arguments put forth by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre about the value of international unionism. I happen to be a member of an international union, and this union to which I belong would be most ineffective in Canada were it not for its international associations. That is a fact. What I mean by the term "Canadian nationalism" is that we should see that the autonomy, not only of the Canadian sections of our unions but also of our legislation, of Canadian law, Canadian control and Canadian rules and regulations pertaining to the freedom of Canadian business, is respected.
It is very apparent to anybody looking at this question that despite what I thought was a certain amount of humour and needling with regard to the Prime Minister meeting President Kennedy on this matter, we have to look at the reality of the United States political associations and at the associations which encircle President Kennedy. If we do that I think we will all see the point that it may be very necessary for the Prime Minister to go directly to Washington, and not to

go there cap in hand. I think we have to recognize that the President is surrounded by a very powerful group of people who, in effect, are not within the congressional framework. One of the bases of the Democratic party's power in the United States and that of President Kennedy, is the very close association he has with some trade union leaders. It is obvious that this is why secretary Wirtz has made the statement he has. It is obvious why there has been all the difficulty in the negotiations; that these labour leaders with whom Mr. Hall is associated are very important to the success or to the power of President Kennedy.
To say this is not to stick one's neck into an American situation, but just to recognize a reality. It seems to me that our Prime Minister has to approach the president and the American people from this point of view. If we are to be sacrificed in terms of interference on the basis of President Kennedy keeping a united front in his political support, then we are in terrible trouble in our association with the United States.
One of the factors which was instrumental last winter, when we had another example of the state department's interference in Canadian affairs, was a sort of follow-up which was reflected in our political campaign, a tremendous fear that maybe we might alienate the Americans. Editorials were written across the country expressing great fears about how we must get along with the Americans and saving that our economies are so interrelated that it would be terrible if we lost their confidence in our dealings with them. It has become very much a partisan political issue. I think the Prime Minister has to realize that it has been recognized, and he can be criticized for the fact, that he took the stand that he has a particular personal association or, if you want to put it, comradeship with the chief executive who governs the United States at this time; that is, in contrast with the previous prime minister of this country.
This, it seems to me, underlies the responsibility he faces at this time in his relationship with the Kennedy administration. Let us not make any mistake about it by assuming we can approach this difficulty as between labour union and labour union and the Minister of Labour and the secretary of labour. The Americans do not operate in this way. Everything focuses upon the top. We tend to hide this fact in our organization, but the Americans never do. I think one thing that is necessary in this particular dispute involving Canadian nationals is a direct approach to President Kennedy to make sure that the consequences of this measure will not be destroyed by the kind of United States

interference of which we have already seen a suggestion. There will be difficulties enough here in Canada in implementing this trusteeship without having to put up with that. One of the reasons we would hope there is fundamental unity in this house about getting the legislation through is just to let the Prime Minister know that he has absolute support in this regard.
One matter which was not touched on by members speaking on the resolution stage is this; I want to mention it here, and I do so because I have had a close relationship with the S.I.U. hiring hall and with members of the union. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George referred to an aspect of it last night when he said there is no doubt that at the present time Banks still has control of the membership of the S.I.U. At least that is what I gathered from what he said. This control, I should like to point out, is not only a bureaucratic control which dictatorial methods have enabled him to deepen. It is a control based on a tremendous respect on the part of members of the S.I.U. I had one conversation with them when I was trying to point out to them that an attack with baseball bats on a man in Fort William in his own home was a kind of action that could not be understood. But these men were justifying it. They were saying well, the guy-I will not go into the obscenities which were used-the guy was a bad character. They could not see that this was not an approach which should be used on anyone who came into conflict with Mr. Banks.
I asked them what it was about Banks they liked. They liked him because he was tough. They told me stories about Banks himself moving in with his fists. You must realize that the kind of person who works on the lakes, the man whose work has so little permanence-a situation which in so many cases is actually fostered by Mr. Banks-has the kind of background and education which gives him great respect for the tough guy.
I asked them whether it did not bother them when they heard the details of Banks living in luxury in Montreal and the fact that he had these Cadillacs and mistresses and things like that. Quite the reverse. Many of them seemed to enjoy a vicarious satisfaction that their guy was doing as well as or better than anyone else in the country. One of them put it "I like to think that our man is doing as well as the guy who owns Canada Steamship Lines". These are the kind of people who are members of the S.I.U. and who give Banks his support.
One of the things we must do, and you cannot do this now, but later, ties up with the newspaper which Banks has used for his
Maritime Transportation Unions own purposes. One of the most important things the trustees will have to do is take control of that newspaper and begin, not with any vindictiveness, to use another approach to convince the members that they can develop some kind of democracy within their union.
In this regard there is something else which appears to me to be of importance, particularly as expressed by the hon. member for Cape Breton South; and this is the inability of some people, it seems to me, to recognize the difference between a corporate structure and the trade union structure as it exists. We expect and demand some kind of democracy from the unions, yet it is very difficult for them to retain democracy; and one of the main difficulties is the attitude of the people who control corporate structures. I have had too many senior executives of companies tell me they like to sit down and deal with one man, a tough character, and hammer out a firm agreement with him. I recall, a few years ago, an executive saying "We don't want to fool around with all these crummy locals where you get involved in wildcats. We want to sit down and talk tough with one guy who has responsibility."
This is why Mr. McLagan refers to Banks as the best paid union leader in Canada. This is why he has such a respect among corporate people. We have to realize that the union structure and the corporate structure have very few similarities, and that the manager or leader of a corporate structure does not give a hoot about the democratic situation in a company or a union; he wants to deal with responsible leaders. And of course Banks can offer the head of a corporation, in his union dealings, a bunch of followers who do exactly what he says.
My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre was quoting the directors of Canada Steamship Lines. I happen to know one of them personally as well as in a business way, Mr. Ambridge, who I understand is a friend of Mr. McLagan. Mr. Ambridge has had excellent relations in his own company in Abitibi. He has gone out of his way, in a sense, to encourage union democracy, and the very fact that he is on the board of directors points up the pressure in a corporate structure when it comes to its attitude toward a democratic union. Here is obviously a case, it seems to me, where the directors of Canada Steamship Lines have ignored the implications of what is involved in dealing in this cosy, face to face situation with a man who has dictatorial control over a union.
I should like to emphasize that this attitude is very much in a way an importation from

Maritime Transportation Unions
the American business scene and the American union scene. A few years ago, not long after I was elected, a knock came on my door one evening. I answered it, and there were about 20 men there, workers on the pipe line. They were all raising cain about conditions. I said to them, "Why don't you go to see your union stewards?" "What union stewards? We don't belong to any union." I said "Well, you do belong to a union if you are working for the pipe line contractor," and I was able to prove it to them. They had belonged to a union for about three months and they had been paying to this union, but they did not know it. The union did not get around to setting up any kind of organization for them. The details had been worked out with the union before the contract had been settled. Some hon. members may wonder why some of us are still bitter about Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, and that is one of the reasons.
When I went to speak to the pipe line contractors they put it down, as they said, in cold turkey. They said "Why should we get involved in all the organizational grievances that develop on the site? When the union comes along we sign a contract and let them deal with the matter. We have dealt with these people all through the United States. The union comes in and sets things up and we never have to worry." This, Mr. Speaker, is the businessman's attitude, the executive attitude. This is the explanation for the fact that, aside from the one shipping company, we have had such a disgraceful response throughout this whole matter from the shipping magnates. I believe this fact needs to be emphasized because somehow people seem to believe, largely as a result of anti-union propaganda, that there must be some kind of democracy in a union, but they tend to apply some different principles of morality to business executives. It is the business executive who, in many ways, is so wrong.
One thing about this legislation that is not very clear, and perhaps it cannot be spelled out, is that the trustees cannot be put at arm's length in their dealings with the membership. I know the hiring hall at Fort William, and it is a well kept, clean place which offers social amenities to the seamen. Unless the trustees are able to have the same kind of contact with the men, the same kind of dealings with the membership and with the men who run that kind of set-up, then the chance of insurrection, of wildcat strikes on the basis of one ship, are likely to multiply. This will make the trusteeship a ridiculous thing. For that reason we would like to emphasize that the trusteeship, and the personnel who man it, must be prepared to not be, in a sense, administrators at arm's


length. We hope they take the attitude that they have the same responsibility that Hal Banks has had, only with a much different moral and ethical approach to their duties.
Initially they have to start with somewhat the same authority Mr. Banks has when he departs, at least I would hope that would be the case. Then they will have to begin the long job of creating and developing some kind of spirit within these men. I would emphasize again that a reasoned, intellectual or academic argument will not have much appeal for the men who work on the lake boats. Since the crucial point in any labour relationship really revolves around the negotiations in settling a contract, the trustees need to be very much aware that it will be in the negotiation of the new contract, as militant representatives of the men dealing with the company, that they will really have to carry the load. If they do not carry it, then the folk memory amongst men like this and their respect for Hal Banks is going to carry on and, in a sense, destroy the trusteeship.
I would hope, too, that in this whole matter, as the trusteeship moves toward what will be their crisis situation, the negotiation of a new contract, the government will try to insure that at the first sign of irresponsibility on the part of the corporation there will be some kind of face to face discussion between government representatives and these companies. I do not want the suggestion to be turned around and have people say that at the next contract negotiations the companies have to cave in, although I do not know that that would be so bad in the light of the way they caved in to Mr. Banks during the last four or five years.
There is on question upon which I should like to hear from the minister. I can see nothing in the bill that refers specifically to this new procedure the S.I.U. adopted in a belated effort to deal with its reputation, that is the setting up of this ex-naval officer as a one man board to hear grievances. I realize that I cannot refer to the bill specifically at this stage, but I should like to suggest it might be wise to retain this office. I do not know anything about the personality of the man, but one of the things that might be very useful in this period of trusteeship is the continuance of that particular office as it relates to the
S.I.U. Perhaps there should even be an expansion of it into a three man board so there may be a possibility for a continuing grievance procedure, particularly in relation to the abuses of the "do not ship" list and things like that. I would carry that into the future in order to give some kind of continuity to the grievance procedure.

In summary, Mr. Speaker, may I say that we are anxious that this bill go through, with the qualifications which were expressed last night as to its timing. We will support the bill and the purposes of the bill. We will support the Prime Minister and the government so long as it shows that it is prepared to make this a very definite issue on which there is no backing down, no caving in, to the kind of pressures we have had revealed already.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, so many of my colleagues in the house, that is learned counsel and some former ministers, have prefaced their speeches with a reference to their long association with the trade union movement that I should like to preface my short interjection by saying that I am also part of the trade union movement. I have been a part of it for a number of years. As a matter of fact this past year, because of the many and varied elections, I have been unable to get back underground to continue my work in the mine. I have certainly been closely associated with unions and realize the feeling of the trade unions when they are told that a Canadian government trusteeship must be imposed upon a section of the labour movement.
While it is true that this procedure appears to be necessary, there seems to be a unanimous feeling that what we are doing is in essence wrong. However, no other alternative seems to be available, and we must impose this trusteeship. Like the hon. member for Timiskaming, I have opposed communists in the trade union movement, that is the political influence of communists and even socialists, and in that connection I have often heard this statement which I thought was attributed to Karl Marx: "The end, after all, justifies the means." I thought this was describing communist philosophy, but just the other day I learned it dated back to a philosopher around the time of the birth of Christ, and it has never been actually established since that the end does justify the means. But somehow or other we have arrived at a situation where, because of the disturbances, rioting and racketeering on the great lakes, this legislation is necessary, and we have to accept the fact that the end in this bill does justify the means.
I know something of the history of Banks and how he came into Canada. As a matter of fact I knew some of the officers of the former Canadian seamen's union, and I understand one or two of them were supposed to be communists or were influenced by Moscow. "Let us rid the unions of communists" became the great battle cry at that time, but now it has been proven there are even worse characters in trade unions than communists.
Maritime Transportation Unions Racketeers of this nature are certainly worse than communists. After all, communism is a political philosophy, while a racketeer operates entirely for his own ends. This should serve to remind us that in what we do today in other fields of organized labour, we cannot be too sure that we will not leave a greater mess-pardon the expression-than the mess we are seeking to clean up.
The hon. member for Port Arthur has suggested that big unions tend to support the government of the United States. I believe all of us feel this is true, but I would draw to his attention that this might also apply in Canada should big unions become the major supporters of any political party. In fact I would warn against either big labour or big business becoming the main supporter of a political party.
I was a bit disturbed yesterday afternoon when the Leader of the Opposition, who after all was the author of the much heralded bill of rights, suggested without apparently a shred of evidence that the officers of the I.L.A. were carrying on the strike on the St. Lawrence in sympathy with Mr. Banks and the S.I.U., and in order to prevent the passage of this bill. This is not guilt by association but rather guilt by coincidence. It just so happens that the members of the I.L.A., after long and protracted negotiations in an attempt to lift themselves out of rather deplorable conditions which have been described by some hon. members of the New Democratic party, found it necessary to resort to strike action. Certainly those conditions which were described are not in tune with the times. It was pointed out that a labourer or stevedore may be called out to work in the morning and then sent home without receiving any pay whatsoever, and certainly time and a half on Saturdays is not out of place in this day and age.
The workers had a justified complaint, and I believe they have gone a long way toward meeting the suggestions of the shipping federation. These men are not of the type described by Mr. Justice Norris. They are not of the type of the Capones, the Hoffas, and that type of racketeer. That description does not apply to them, and I think it was quite improper for the Leader of the Opposition to make that suggestion simply because their strike coincided with efforts to settle the great lakes dispute.
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour have expressed their concern about the statements made by Mr. Wirtz and Mr. Meany with respect to the legislation now before this house. In my opinion the best answer we in this house can make to those statements is for each and every one of us to stand up before one o'clock and be counted unanimously in favour of this legislation.

Maritime Transportation Unions

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether it will be possible for the members of the house to stand up and be counted on this legislation before one o'clock, because it was the Minister of Labour himself who suggested, when he introduced the resolution preceding the bill the other day, that there might be those in the house keenly interested in this unprecedented action who would wish to withhold what they had to say until they had the actual legislation in front of them. He also gave the assurance that once the bill was before us we could speak on second reading on matters which we might otherwise have covered on the resolution stage.
I was one of those members who accepted the suggestion and the commitment of the minister, and that is why I am speaking on second reading, having read the bill now before us. I of course have no desire to hold it up, but there are certain matters regarding trade unionism, the record of trade unionism, and parliamentary legislation to deal with internal affairs of the trade union movement that should be discussed in principle.
So far as I am concerned it is rather imperative that I do so, because I have been a member of an international trade union since 1924. From 1924, at which time due to the existing constitution of the union I could not be a full member because I had to come under the apprenticeship clause. Until 1933 I can say I was an active member of that trade union. From 1933 to 1963 I have not been what may be called in the normal sense an active member of a trade union. If I may put it this way, from 1924 to 1933 I was a member of a trade union because of my occupation, and from 1933 to 1963 I have been by profession an elected member of parliamentary bodies, provincial and federal. But I still maintain my interest in the trade union movement. From 1924 to 1933 I was active in a trade union, but from 1933 to 1963 I have acquired a greater experience and understanding of the trade union movement because in that period of time I had the privilege and opportunity of meeting not only the rank and file members but those in the trade union movement holding official positions. I have also been a member of arbitration boards more than once on behalf of trade unions, and have also attended trade union conventions.
I thought it necessary to outline this background to explain why I felt impelled to speak on second reading of the bill. The trade union movement is one of the most marvellous organizations of democracy that the world

has ever known. It operates not only in the economic field but recognizes the democracy of parliament. The trade union movement only asks the democracy of parliament, be it the House of Commons or a provincial legislature, for the protection of its inherent democratic rights. Beyond that, however, the trade union movement-I will not say "opposed"-has always been fearful of parliamentary action to interfere with what are basically trade union principles and the internal operations and privileges of the trade union movement.
That is understandable, Mr. Speaker, because if you look at the interference of parliamentary authority as evidenced by certain legislation in British Columbia and Newfoundland you can understand the fear of the trade union movement as to the possibility of their internal rights and privileges being interfered with by law if there happens to be a government or governments which are anti-labour.
With that background I now come to the situation which we in the House of Commons face at the present time. As a member of the trade union movement since 1924, and still paying my dues, I want to say that the situation we now face is not only disturbing to the members of the House of Commons, who I feel do not want to interfere, but is most disturbing to the trade union movement itself. As was pointed out by the federal leader of the New Democratic party and emphasized by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, we face extraordinary legislation because of an extraordinary situation. If there is one thing that the trade union movement does not want and will try to avoid it is parliamentary decision on a trade union matter.
To me as a member of an international trade union since 1924 there is nothing we hate to see more than that, but we in this group are prepared to face up to the issue. In so doing however, we want recognition of why this situation has been brought about, and recognition that the trusteeship must be removed as speedily as possible. Although I was prepared a day ago to go along with the decision of this group, I must say that I did so with a feeling of regret; but after what has been made evident in statements by the government of the United States and by the president of the A.F.L.-C.I.O. I now go along with this legislation enthusiastically, and I hope to explain my reasons a little later.
May I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate very much that hon. members allowed me some eight minutes this morning to give the background with regard to why I felt it imperative I should speak on second reading of the most important bill now before us. Just prior to the luncheon adjournment I said that after the recess I would explain why until yesterday it was with some reluctance I felt I had to support the bill and why, in view of the developments in the past 24 hours, I now have no reluctance and will support it wholeheartedly.
May I add to some of the statements I made this morning before I give those reasons. Over the years in Canada our trade union movement has had what is known as national unions and international unions. In the past few years particularly reactionary politicians, reactionary editorial writers and a great many employers have been attacking international unions in Canada on the ground that they are controlled outside of Canada. Some years ago there may have been-I say "may have been"-some basis for that argument, but not for many years now.
In my 30 years as an elected member and 39 years as a trade unionist I have come into contact with hundreds of locals throughout Canada and many local, provincial, national and international trade union leaders. I can say without fear of honest contradiction that by far the greater majority of Canadian trade unions are autonomous, so much so that over the past few years international union constitutions have been changed at international conventions to make it clear that Canadian unions of an international nature have complete autonomy, and even some unions that have not done so by international constitutional change have arrived at an understanding that international trade unions in Canada have complete autonomy.
That is why the extraordinary statement made by Mr. Meany less than 24 hours ago is the greatest betrayal of the international trade movement that that movement has known in the history of North America because by his statement, made without knowledge, understanding or authority, he gives support to the lie that the trade union movement in Canada, in which I include myself because I am a member of a union, does not have complete autonomy.
I said before the luncheon adjournment that I would outline why I am giving complete support to the bill. First, we have the situation where an imported United States trade union gangster, racketeer and goon squad leader has brought about a reign of 28902-5-220
Maritime Transportation Unions terror, intimidation, beatings, shootings and bombings in one of our major industries, and no responsible trade unionist or member of the House of Commons can allow that to continue. Second, despite all the efforts of the trade union movement and in particular the Canadian Labour Congress over the years they have been unable to resolve the problem on the basis of its being one of internal trade union administration. Third, every effort by the Canadian Labour Congress and the government of Canada to find a solution has been made impossible by certain United States government authorities' interference in consultation, if not in conspiracy, with reactionary trade union leaders, Mr. Meany and Mr. Paul Hall.
And fourth, that the Canadian trade union movement and the parliament of Canada cannot and will not accept outside domination of our jurisdiction and sovereignty, whether it be in the trade union or in the parliamentary field.
Never in my 30 years of parliamentary life and my 39 years of trade union life would I have thought it necessary, Mr. Speaker, to speak in this way; but this is a matter which has to be faced by all men who take on responsibility. As I have said, I have been a member of an international union for 39 years, and with that background I say it must be made clear by this House of Commons, as it has also been made clear by Claude Jodoin and the C.L.C. executive, to the governmental authorities of the United States and such trade union authorities as Mr. Meany and Paul Hall, that they must keep their sticky fingers out of our Canadian business-and I mean sticky fingers. May I say through you, Mr. Speaker-I doubt whether what I say means anything in the United States but I will say it anyway-that Mr. Meany should be told that he has set back the trade union movement in Canada perhaps 20 years by his interference in our trade union affairs, without any knowledge or understanding of them or basis of responsibility. He has played into the hands of our reactionary editorial writers and politicians and has made it more difficult for those of us who know the truth to insist on the autonomy of the Canadian trade union movement.
Others more capable than I at the resolution stage, Mr. Speaker, from the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) to the leaders of parties and others, have pointed out what we in this House of Commons, which is the sovereign body of Canada, are doing today, and perhaps tomorrow and Monday, might bring about serious consequences. That may be so, but I want to say with all the emphasis of which I am capable that if the

Maritime Transportation Unions government of the United States through its labour department, and the reactionary leadership of the A.F.L.-C.I.O. through Mr. Meany, want to challenge the trade union sovereignty of Canada as well as the parliamentary sovereignty of Canada by taking any action in the United States, trade unionwise, conti-nentalwise, nationalwise or parliamentarywise, to deny and to defy our rights, then God help Canada if we do not accept that challenge.
I also say that both the government of the United States and the trade union movement in the United States as expressed by Mr. Meany should realize this, that if they challenge our exports and our ships because we utilize our sovereign power, they may find it hurts them more than it hurts us, because we are the biggest importer of goods from the United States. To the best of my knowledge, for the first time in the history of this country we have had this extraordinary conspiracy by reactionary trade union leaders and labour representatives in the United States trying to interfere-not only trying but succeeding in their attempt to negate the trade union authority of Canada and the sovereignty of our parliament. I want to express the hope that the government will stand firm on the maintenance of our sovereignty and parliamentary system and tradition. I want to pay my heartfelt respects to Mr. Claude Jodoin and the executive of the C.L.C. for insisting on maintaining a position which will solve our own problems in Canada within the trade union movement, without outside influence or domination.
I cannot sit down, Mr. Speaker, without expressing what I think all of us feel in our hearts, and that is the terrific respect we have for the trade unions of Canada which have been found completely innocent by Mr. Justice Norris of any wrongdoing. We have the finest commendation from Mr. Justice Norris of the way they work as trade unionists. Our trade unions of Canada have agreed, much as they dislike it, to come under a trusteeship, the creation of which is unprecedented and is an interference in trade union affairs, if this means peace in our sea ports and on the great lakes. This is a matter which should not be forgotten, sir; it is the one found guilty which refuses, while those found innocent are prepared to go along with the wishes of the people of Canada, as expressed through their elected representatives to the House of Commons.
I do not think I need say more, Mr. Speaker. As I say, I dislike this legislation; we all dislike it; but in view of all the circumstances and the extraordinary situation which has developed in our country, and in

view of the challenge to the trade unions and parliament of Canada in the form of domination by a foreign power, we have no other alternative to take, and I hope we will all be unanimous in supporting the bill before us. However, I sincerely hope the government will recognize that they can "sell" this legislation, both psychologically and by public relations, a lot better if they make the one specific change I have referred to, namely, change the limit to two years, which period can be extended if required. I think that that one change will help bring a greater understanding to the people of the country, and particularly to our trade unionists, of the fact that this is only a temporary measure for two years instead of five.
In closing, may I say I appreciate the courtesy of this house in allowing me to speak for this length of time.

speechtext:
I intend to speak only briefly, but after a careful perusal of the terms of the bill I rise to express my opposition to it on the following grounds: first, because in my opinion it is wrong in principle, period. In my opinion it violates the spirit and purpose of the Canadian Bill of Rights. Second, I oppose it because I think it transgresses established trade union principles which have been recognized throughout Canada to date.
I oppose it also because I believe that in order for it to be effective it must have the support of the great majority of the rank and file of the trade union movement in Canada. As a result of discussions I have had, and as a result of correspondence and telegrams I have received, I am convinced that there is massive opposition to this bill among the rank and file of the trade union movement in this country, and that this opposition is growing daily.
I also believe that if this bill is to be effective it must have the support of the United States government. It is apparent from recent statements made by the secretary of labour, Mr. Wirtz, that we cannot expect any cooperation in the administration of this legislation from that direction. I am sure that as Canadians we all resent this attitude on the part of the United States secretary of labour. I am one who resents it very much indeed. Unfortunately, however, we have to face facts, and when it comes to the administration of this legislation it cannot be effective unless we receive the co-operation of the government of the United States. This must be so because of the very nature of the industry involved.
I oppose this measure also because I believe that in order to be effective it must receive the co-operation of the trade union movement in the United States for the very same reason

as I have just given, namely the nature of this industry. It all presents a most difficult problem indeed in the absence of this cooperation. It is obvious from the statement yesterday by Mr. Meany that we cannot expect the co-operation of at least the leaders of essential sections of the trade union movement in the United States in the administration of this legislation; yet, as I say this cooperation is essential if the present measure is to be effective. Once again, like the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) I resent this attempt at interference on the part of Mr. Meany and the attitude taken toward this important problem by the head of an important trade union organization in the United States. Nevertheless, once again we have to face the facts and I am sure the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) will admit that this legislation cannot be administered successfully without the co-operation of the United States government and of those sections of the labour movement in the United States which are directly concerned.
Another reason for my opposition to this bill is that it completely overlooks-has cast aside, as it were-the common sense and democratic strength of the trade union movement in Canada. The rank and file of the trade union movement here have never been presented with this challenge-and I admit it is a challenge-in union affairs to correct the situation which has arisen within their own house. It has been demonstrated that this type of situation can be met by trade unions. It has been done on the Pacific coast. Some hon. members may recall the unpleasant Northland incident. They will also note that there has been very little violence, very few difficulties, in the shipping industry on that coast. In fact we have seen little of the violence which was foreshadowed at one time. Why? It is because the trade union movement in Vancouver would not stand for that nonsense. When the S.I.U. threatened violence and undemocratic practices, its leaders had to pull in their horns because of the action of other trade unionists in the city of Vancouver who accepted their responsibility as Canadians. A good example of this is the Northland affair in which the unions united against the S.I.U. At that time there were hints in the press about violence and all the danger surrounding this situation. These forecasts were not realized because a good number of the unions, supported by the rank and file of their membership, kept a constant vigil on the Northland situation by picketing 24 hours a day. These members of trade unions volunteered their services without thought of remuneration in defence of trade union democratic principles and practice 28902-5-220J
Maritime Transportation Unions established in this country. They were successful in their efforts, and the S.I.U. gangsters, if there were any around at that time, stayed in their holes and did not appear. Thus, a serious situation in Vancouver was corrected because the trade unions met the challenge themselves and dealt with it from within their own ranks. I think the government has lost an opportunity to present this challenge to the trade union movement. I believe we are underestimating the democratic strength of that movement in Canada and its understanding of the working of free institutions, whether in the union movement or here in parliament. I reach this view after conversations I have had with a number of trade unionists-good, honest people who are firm supporters of the trade union movement and who are strongly opposed to this legislation while, at the same time recognizing the responsibility which the trade unions face today to do something about the present situation.
I urge the government to reconsider this legislation and provide an opportunity for the trade unions in this country to mobilize the tremendous reservoir of democratic understanding, ability and native common sense they possess so that they themselves may have an opportunity to correct this situation in defence of democratic trade union principles and our Canadian way of life. Once again, I urge the government to reconsider the passage of this bill. I ask it to trust the working people of Canada to correct this situation, which they will, if given an opportunity.
