speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in opening my remarks I would call the attention of the house to the fact that this statement was in no way associated with the bill that is before us. I do not wish to prolong the matter that is before the house. That should bring a cheer. I would, however, ask, as did the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), that every consideration be given to this question before the government pushes it any further. An appeal was made in this house last night by several hon. members that we keep cool heads about this. I thought at the time this perhaps implied that I was rather excited about it. But I would ask each and every hon. member in this house whether they have given every consideration to the repercussions that may develop should Mr. Meany and Mr. Wirtz have their way and if the statements they have made receive the backing of the unions throughout the United States. Have hon. members considered the repercussions; and if so, why the haste?
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr Winch), I think it was, made a statement to the effect that Mr. Meany's remarks of last evening have set the trade union movement back 20 years. There must be some doubt in that particular hon. member's mind, because as I see it, if this trusteeship were to be successful it would be a step forward

for the trade union movement. I can only see Mr. Meany's statement setting the trade union movement back 20 years if the trusteeship fails. I agree that we should keep cool heads about this and should give every consideration to the repercussions that could develop from a failure of the trusteeship.
It has also been pointed out on several occasions that five unions are going to come under the trusteeship, four of them voluntarily. Knowing something of the workings of trade unions and trade union leaders, I think I can speak with some authority on this question. I referred last night to the trouble within the trade unions these days being that there are too many professionals in them. By professionals I mean men who have reached the top in particular trade unions and who at no time were ever associated with the particular work involved in that union. In other words, they have gone in as professional organizers and have reached the upper echelons of the executives of different unions, and they do not have a complete understanding of the rank and file members under them. It has been said that four unions have voluntarily or willingly agreed to come under this trusteeship. And why not? In the case of these four unions their doing this provides them with the very thing they have been struggling to get for a number of years; that is, rid themselves of Mr. Hal Banks and his union. They have everything to gain and nothing to lose by accepting this voluntarily. It is not for individuals in this house to set themselves up as judges with regard to what the rank and file members of trade unions in this country may think. But I think it is the duty of every hon. member in this house to express his feelings about trade unions and this particular trusteeship.
I would further ask the government to give consideration to the particular spot in which they have placed these trustees. In view of the actions of Mr. Banks and his goons in the last few years I believe these men will be placed in a very precarious position. There is no doubt that Mr. Banks and his goon squads have gone about this country attacking people in their own homes. I think they have even gone so far as to beat up pregnant women. What is to stop them intimidating and possibly doing bodily harm to the trustees who will be appointed by this government? What is to stop Mr. Banks from spreading his goon tactics?

Maritime Transportation Unions I could not refer to the Norris commission report, but I would call the government's attention to the recommendations on page 311 under the heading "Prosecutions". I think if these had been put into effect previously Mr. Banks would today be in the position he should be in, namely behind bars, where he could do no harm to anyone. The deportation of Mr. Banks or dealing with Mr. Banks in any other way than putting him behind bars will not erase the fact that he will be able to operate in the same way that he has operated in the past, from any location to which he may go in the future. If he is deported he can go across to Buffalo, or to some other area, and carry on his goon tactics just as well from that side of the border as he has from this side. There is only one remedy for Mr. Banks, and that is to put him in a place where he can do no harm. I believe that if this government had taken the initiative and acted on the Norris commission report which recommended prosecution of Mr. Banks, rather than adopting the recommendation to set up a trusteeship, it is quite possible that the trade union movement would not have been faced with this trusteeship. I deplore the continued reference to the free trade union movement, in view of the fact that this trusteeship is now going to be imposed.
Why were those recommendations of Mr. Justice Norris not followed out? Why were the prosecutions not instituted? As I have said before, if this trusteeship is set up, and apparently it is going to be, then members of this house will look to the minister for a report on how this trusteeship is working. We will have the minister rising day after day, as ministers do in connection with so many other agencies in this country, and tell us that he is awaiting a report. As soon as he receives it, he will give it to the house. Then, the following week there will be similar questions and a similar answer will be given. The members of this house will be unable to receive answers to questions about this trusteeship and how it is working. If initiative had been taken on the first recommendation and Mr. Banks had been prosecuted, it is quite possible that today the future would hold brighter prospects than it does when we consider the imposition of trusteeship on the trade unions of this country.
Now, a request has been made by the leader of the Canadian Labour Congress that the trusteeship be restricted to the maritime unions. Well, there is nothing wrong with that request. However, let no one say this is not a precedent. We are going to have a hard time making that statement stick. Let any trade union become involved in a dispute in the future, and someone will come to the

Maritime Transportation Unions government and ask for the imposition of a similar trusteeship. Reference can be made to this as a precedent. No amount of talk can get around the fact that you are, for the first time in any English speaking country, imposing trusteeship upon the free trade unions. The precedent will be established, and you can look for trouble in this field in the future. In fact, if such a trusteeship had been in effect a couple of years ago, something could have developed in the Sudbury area where there were charges flung back and forth between two unions in connection with raiding. This is much the same type of situation.
Again, I say hon. members are not too sure about this. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) said a few minutes ago that he was in full support of this trusteeship, but he is not too sure that it is going to work. I am not too sure about it, either. I hope I am proven wrong. There is nothing I would hope for more than that this trusteeship would be successful. As I have said, especially following the statements by Mr. Wirtz and Mr. Meany, I cannot believe this is going to prove successful in any way, shape or form. I repeat what I said last night, that in order to make this trusteeship work, full agreement and co-operation between the gov-enment of the United States and the government of Canada will be required. Without this full co-operation, no trusteeship is going to work.
As I have said, hon. members who support this measure are not too sure that it is going to be successful, but they are willing to support it. I refer to the remarks just made by the hon. member for Vancouver East. He said that the statement by Mr. Meany had set the Canadian labour movement back 20 years. This is only true in part, because I see this as a great forward step if it proves to be successful. If it does not prove to be successful, then the hon. member is correct and this labour movement is set back 20 years. Most hon. members who have supported this trusteeship have, at the same time, expressed doubt that it will ever work. In going along with these other members, I would sincerely ask the government to give consideration to the repercussions that will follow if the trusteeship does not work. The chances of its working now are only 50-50. I think that a concentrated effort should be made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the President of the United States to assure that, if this trusteeship is necessary, then the necessary protection and service will be given to Canadian ships visiting United States ports.

listened to statements to the effect that Mr. Banks is a criminal, yet we find that Mr. Banks is still free in this country. I feel this trusteeship will not settle anything, if our syndicates as well as our workingmen are still at the mercy of some United States union leaders who, in my opinion, may have given orders which would cause Canada trouble in trying to deliver goods that have been sold to other countries in the world. If this is so, then I think it is time the government took strong action against these outsiders, who are trying to tell us in Canada what to do.

Mr. Speaker, we give our support to union members everywhere in Canada, but we are strongly opposed to certain union leaders who, instead of showing some respect for workers, are exploiting them shamelessly, as is the case within the union we are discussing at the present time.
Certain union leaders, as everybody knows, are paid more than the President of the United States and seem to have things pretty much their own way in labour-management relations. It is time we found out whether those individuals are organizing or disorganizing labour.
Our Canadian workers are not revolutionaries, but some union leaders are. The case of Hal Banks shows quite clearly that we must remain continually on the alert in our relations with such people.
Mr. Speaker, the government should take the necessary steps to encourage in every way possible those unions which are essentially Canadian.
We must stop, in labour unions and elsewhere, taking orders from foreigners who know nothing about our needs concerning labour, production, planning and the economy.
I feel the government would be giving substantial assistance to labour unions if it recognized only worthy representatives and essentially Canadian unions which would be contributing to the development of our national economy.

As is evident in the preamble to the bill, and as is evident from the Norris inquiry upon which the bill in a sense is based, the purpose of this action is not to put free trade unions under trusteeship. The purpose of this action is to restore freedom and democratic practices in the principal trade union that will be affected by this trusteeship.
The additional four trade unions which will be under this trusteeship have willingly accepted, without any pressure or coercion, their inclusion within the trusteeship in the interests of cleaning up this situation. Surely the leaders of these four unions realize what free trade unionism means? Surely they understand the established trade union principles that have been mentioned by hon. members? Yet, notwithstanding these considerations they have of their own volition accepted what might be called this sacrifice in the interests of restoring democracy and freedom to the seamen who are presently denied these practices. That is the purpose of the legislation.
It is also a fact that after careful study and soul-searching the executive committee of the Canadian Labour Congress, and later the executive council of the congress, accepted the necessity of this action and agreed to co-operate with the purposes of the trusteeship. Surely these men understand free trade unionism and established free trade union principles, yet they have said that this is a necessary act to be taken.
Hon. gentlemen have expressed reluctance about the action now proposed, but there is no one more reluctant, or has been more reluctant, to undertake this action than I, because it is unprecedented and extraordinary. But it is done because of the extraordinary difficulties that existed and because no effective alternative had been presented. We did search vigorously for an effective alternative, an inter-union arrangement, but I think hon. gentlemen will agree with me that it was right and proper for the government and the Canadian Labour Congress to refuse an inter-union agreement with the arrangements that had been proposed.
We were willing to pay a price for a private arrangement, in the sense that it would depend upon the consent of many elements in the trade union situation whom we would expect to act in good faith. We were willing to assume good faith, and ready to accept an
Maritime Transportation Unions inter-union arrangement; but surely it was wrong to ask that a Canadian problem should not be determined by Canadians in the final analysis. That was the basic ground for this refusal, combined with the fact that there was no clear provision that the trusteeship could act effectively in given situations when the third person and his nationality were undetermined.
No one who contributed to this debate has proposed an alternative to this action. No one has proposed an alternative that would deal with the situation. That is a fact; and when the Norris commission report came out and the trustee recommendation was under consideration we always came back to the question, what is the alternative to a public trusteeship? No alternative has proved possible, and that is why the government is taking this action.
It is a fact that the trustees can deal with the situation in Canada. What happens in the United States is a matter for the United States government and union leaders in the United States, who are themselves committed to the proposition of civil rights for all trade unionists. In this situation we must rely on and expect co-operation in the United States in order that this trusteeship be made fully effective.
Today the Prime Minister made a statement on behalf of the government with respect to statements made yesterday in Washington. speechtext:
I should like to add a word to the discussion on this very important subject. It is with reluctance that a trusteeship is proposed over trade unions. The rights of labour are an important part of human rights and fundamental freedoms. Free trade unions flourish in a free society. The purpose of the present bill is not to abridge the rights of labour to organize and to be democratically represented, but to ensure that these rights are protected.
I am reminded of a story told by a southern senator of a fellow who clenched his fists and went down the street swinging his arms. He hit a bystander on the nose. The bystander protested, and the fellow said, "I have a right to swing my arms." The bystander said, "Yes, you have a right to swing your arms, but where my nose begins your rights end."
In exercising its authority on the great lakes, Mr. Chairman, a union has been denying many workers human rights and fundamental freedoms. Acts of terror have been rampant. Men have been dragged off ships, assaulted on the streets, harassed, beaten, bullied, crushed into submission. Raids have been conducted on other unions and their machinery of operation brutally appropriated. In all this struggle over a period of years, where have been the forces of law and order? Why have culprits not been apprehended and dealt with by our courts? How could this state of lawlessness proceed without lawful retribution? Certainly, the guilt is even wider than the union which has been indicted in the court of public opinion.
If, in the past, federal authorities performed their duties in maintaining the laws of this country, how could the government have received a letter from a shipping company acknowledging that it had been bullied into an agreement with a union in defiance of the laws of Canada, without action being taken? What about provincial authorities? The administration of justice is a special responsibility of the provincial governments. How could these lawless events have persisted over a period of years while the guardians of the law turned aside from their duties?

Maritime Transportation Unions
This government has been most wise in exhausting the possibilities for a private settlement. An agreed solution that was both strong and effective, such as the Minister of Labour has assured the house he has sought, would be much preferable. The imposition of trusteeship on trade unions, even for a short duration, is not a happy solution. We need the co-operation of the international trade union movement, since our trade unions are generally part of a Canadian-United States structure, and because our ships are sailing in international waters. If we are denied this support, many pitfalls are open. We could be faced with a challenge from sister unions across the border.
It would be helpful to have the support of the United States administration. In addition, there is suspicion of public trusteeship within Canadian trade unions themselves. More especially, for all of these reasons, it has been necessary for the government to seek patiently for a voluntary and effective solution within the trade union movement. And now, if a government trusteeship is to be imposed, it is important, not only that justice be done but, as wise judges have said, that justice appears to be done. The patient search for an effective voluntary agreement was the path of wisdom. The government, in following this statesmanlike course, is to be commended.
The craft trade union movement of Canada, from the days of Samuel Gompers and the knights of labour, is one of continental growth, and leadership has come first from the United States. In addition, the contribution of John L. Lewis and the united mine workers of America in the development of industrial trade unionism leaves the Canadian unions much in their debt. Many important and progressive craft and industrial unions have provided the core of our trade union movement. Their responsibility is a hallmark of our democracy. The present struggle can be an important turning point in trade unionism on this continent. The voice of the Canadian Labour Congress has not prevailed in the councils of the A.F.L.-C.I.O. in matters concerning Canadian labour.
We may now see a polarization of continental unionism, and a more independent Canadian movement. We are witnessing a failure of continental leadership. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has praised the accommodation within the Canadian Labour Congress of national and international unions. I cannot be as sanguine as he that this era will return. It is a surprising thing that the leaders of the A.F.L.-C.I.O. did not go all out to accommodate the Canadian Labour Congress in setting up a private


union trusteeship. The leadership of the international movement is strongly opposed to government intervention and the Canadian Labour Congress was available to serve. Thus, they could have their cake and eat it, provided the preservation of the status quo on the great lakes, or something approaching the status quo, was not their aim.
The report of Mr. Justice Norris is not as helpful as it might have been. He has proposed serious procedures, but has not examined them. An analysis by the commissioner of the constitutional and other practical problems facing a government trusteeship was certainly called for. Did Mr. Justice Norris consult the very able counsel of the royal commission in formulating his report?
In this country, we want to see a free, strong, independent trade union movement give effective leadership in the many important areas of industrial and public life, where labour in Canada has shown such responsibility. The surest guarantee of wise government trusteeship is that the trustees should be reluctant to assume their jobs, anxious to complete their work well and effectively, and return the affairs of the unions to their members, where they belong.

Mr. Chairman, this is an extraordinary remedy, but I assume it is directed towards an extraordinary situation. Nevertheless such legislation, no matter what evil it may tend to be directed towards, must be founded on proper constitutional grounds, and this is the point I would now like to make.
I should say to the minister through you, sir, that this is an issue which is raised in the preamble, which has been referred to by the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam, and it may well be raised at a later point; but as I bring it to the minister's attention at this stage perhaps he can deal with it now or later.
I first call to the attention of the committee the fact that on August 2, as reported at page 2943 of Hansard for that date, this matter was brought up by the Leader of the Opposition

who asked whether the government was concerning itself with the introduction of legislation to implement recommendations of the Norris commission.
Dealing with the question of when the legislation would be introduced the Prime Minister said:
It would be impossible in the circumstances to have this difficult and complicated legislation prepared within a matter of weeks. It may require a strict examination of the constitutionality of the legislation-
-which I thought was a very sensible observation.
In the preamble to the bill I note these words in the first paragraph:
It was indicated-
-referring back to the report-
-that within the shipping industry in Canada an emergency situation has developed that endangers navigation and shipping on the St. Lawrence seaway with a consequent threat to the economy of Canada, the international relations of Canada, and peace, order and good government on the St. Lawrence seaway-
It may well be, and the minister may be able to answer this, that because the federal government has in the past occupied the field of labour relations with regard to matters which are under the competent jurisdiction of the federal government, that occupation permits it to proceed with this legislation by itself, and to pass legislation which may, and probably does to some extent, invade the property and civil rights jurisdiction which was allocated to provincial governments. But, I am concerned with the fact that the government may be attempting to break new ground here by using the words "an emergency situation has developed" in a particular sector of the country, and making reference to the "peace, order and good government" in a particular section of the country.
As you are aware, Mr. Chairman, the British North America Act in section 91 does provide that the federal government may, among other things, "make laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada," but I have never understood this to mean that, should an emergency develop in any one part of Canada, the federal government may legislate in matters not otherwise in its legislative competence. I think this has been held in cases which dealt with emergency legislation following world war I. I am not going to refer to the cases, but there are very definite limitations on the extent to which the federal government may legislate under the guise of an emergency. I think this applies also to the right to legislate in respect to the making of laws "for the peace, order and good government of Canada."
I am not offering this in any spirit of mischief, but in passing legislation of this kind 28902-5-2214
Maritime Transportation Unions we should be assured by the minister, particularly in the light of what was said by the Prime Minister on August 2, of the basis on which this legislation is founded, and if in effect the constitutional authority is either on the ground of the right of the federal government, having dealt with labour legislation in federal matters, to pass this particular act, or whether the use of these words in the first paragraph of the preamble are significant, and the government is attempting to found the legality of this enactment because an emergency situation has developed in one part of the country and there is a desire to pass laws for the "peace, order and good government on the St. Lawrence seaway." If this is the case, then this is a matter which will require some consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to hold up this bill. Hon. members of this group have indicated that we support the principle, but this is the first occasion that we can express our very great objection to the fact that this legislation is discriminatory. It has bean said that justice must not only be done but it must also appear to be done.
One thing becomes clear from reading the Norris report and that is that the maritime industry is in trouble not just because one of the trade unions was controlled by a gangster, Banks, but because a big shipping company was willing to work with that union and with Banks. I do not know if the minister has read the whole report, but in one section Mr. Norris quotes Mr. Dunkerley, after counsel for the commission had questioned the other shipping companies about the difficulties they had encountered with prayer meetings which were used to disrupt their orderly operations, and Mr. Dunkerley makes it very clear that Canada Steamship Lines never had prayer meetings.
Mr. Dunkerley also says that any time they had trouble they could get quick results by going to the top, to Banks. Another thing which is evident to anybody who can read and think, is that Mr. Banks never did anything for nothing. If Banks gave a favour to somebody he got a service in return.
I join with other hon. members in expressing the hope that the government will quit its delay and get on with the processing of the report of the special counsel appointed to inquire into the possibilities of bringing prosecutions against Banks and the shipping companies involved.
Now, however, we get a bill to enact the maritime transportation unions trustees act, and after two days of discussion and after at least half a dozen members have spoken about the faults of one particular shipping company, the minister completely ignores
3462	HOUSE OF
Maritime Transportation Unions those remarks. Does he feel that the shipping companies are free of guilt, or does he feel this is not the place to mention it? Will there be prosecutions and will the shipping act be amended? The committee deserves to know these things. The labour unions of Canada, which on the whole are clean, deserve to know from the minister what he intends to do. Are we going to have in 1963, as we have had so often in the past, prosecutions and a clamping down on trade unions while people in power, with money and influence, get off scot-free? The people of Canada are entitled to an explanation.

subtopic: MARITIME TRANSPORTATION UNIONS
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have listened to a great deal from all sides of the house, all favourable to this legislation. The house, in a most impressive display of unanimity, has endorsed a far reaching piece of legislation which I am sure is repugnant in principle to very many hon. members. I can recall the chairman of the war labour board in the United States saying the state must be very careful before it displays its own naked power. In a situation like this we are using the powers of the state to achieve a purpose which must be achieved.
I am very proud indeed of the Minister of Labour, the caution with which he has approached this matter and the thoroughness with which he has investigated all the ramifications before action was taken. There are those who felt that the government should have rushed into action before now. There are others, such as the hon. member for Port Arthur, to whom I listened with a great deal of attention, who gave us an insight into the reasons why the parties to this dispute have been led to the positions they have taken.
Nevertheless the public interest is paramount. The time has come when we all recognize that we must take the step of using the power of the state to dispossess a union leader, whom all of us have come to recognize as an evil force in organized labour. We believe in free collective bargaining. We believe in leaving as much as possible to the free determination of unions and management within the framework that has been evolved for the solution of labour disputes.
This is a situation that goes beyond the normal circumstances of collective bargaining. This is a situation in which the unusual and far reaching action of imposing a government trusteeship has been adopted by, as I said, a rare display of unanimity in this chamber.
It would be foolish indeed to think that by simply adopting this legislation we can anticipate that certain results will follow. There is a very great burden upon those chosen as trustees. As was indicated before, the testing


point will come when negotiations for a contract reached their final stage. What kind of contract will be worked out? What kind of democratic union will be worked out within the framework of the trusteeship? What will be the conclusion of the trusteeship? How will it terminate? How will we guarantee that at the end of the period of government operation of not only one union but a group of unions we will have evolved a democratic structure which will be welcomed by the same unions within the ranks of Canadian organized labour that have welcomed government action in these circumstances?
This dispute has taken on an international aspect that again is a little repugnant. I cannot add to what has been said so very well by the Prime Minister, the Leader of the Opposition and the spokesmen for the other parties. There is a challenge to our right to govern ourselves as Canadians within Canadian institutions, and we are seeking to assert this right through this measure. We are confident at the same time that the administration of this measure will be in accordance with the principles of democratic collective bargaining, fully respecting the rights of the parties to the dispute. We are under no illusion with regard to the potential dangers of this task but there is no other choice before us.

Mr. Chairman, I think that the committee is entitled to hear my reasons for voting against second reading of the bill and I wish to take this opportunity to put those reasons on record, so there will be no misunderstanding. In order to avoid repetition may I say at the outset that I endorse fully the remarks made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South who voted with me on this side of the house against the measure. The views expressed by him would have been expressed by me had I spoken on second reading.
I too express surprise at the parliamentar; secretary to the Minister of Labour voting for the measure, since he is a member of the same union that I and the hon. member for Kootenay West, I believe, are, and since that union, the mine-mill union, has expressed the view that this is a problem which the workers themselves should clear up without the imposition of legislation that imposes upon their freedom. When the parliamentary secretary spoke to the thirteenth convention of the mine-mill union in Sudbury last September he singled out the fact, as reported in the latest issue of the Mine-Mill Herald, that mine-mill was the first international union to endorse the principle of Canadian autonomy for its Canadian section. He stated, and here

I quote the Mine-Mill Herald which has the words in quotation marks:
"This is a move I believe others envy particularly at this moment."
I would assume that implicit in those remarks was a reference to the situation on the great lakes which was confronting the government.
The basic reasons for my not finding it possible to support the measure on second reading are these. I believe that the powers given to the government trustees are much too broad, if they are required at all, a matter concerning which I will have a word or two to say in a moment. I believe the legislation is unconstitutional since in my view it interferes with the property and civil rights of citizens and goes beyond the scope of the powers of this parliament. I believe also that the establishment of a board of trustees with the prime purpose ostensibly to shunt Banks out of his position of power is not going to solve the situation at all. I believe, as the hon. member for Cape Breton South said, that this legislation is going to cause more difficulties than the government is already faced with because I believe we are embarking on an international war between the American sections of the maritime unions and the Canadian sections. I think this is particularly so, because as I understand the intention of the government two Canadian trustees and one American will be appointed. The minister shakes his head so I assume this is not the case. I can only proceed on the assumption that there are going to be two American trustees and one Canadian trustee, which makes the situation even worse.

speechtext:
This simply points up the validity of my fears and those of the hon. member for Cape Breton South, and others who have spoken against the measure, that international strife will develop particularly because of the exclusion of the Americans.
I think that one thing which perhaps might have been done, as suggested by the Leader of the Opposition, was to seek the assurance of Mr. Wirtz that there would be United States co-operation, a question which I do not believe was answered by the Minister of Labour. Apart from his reading a paragraph of the statement made by Mr. Wirtz, he has given us no assurance at all that he has consulted with Mr. Wirtz to obtain from him an unassailable guarantee that co-operation on the part of the United States government and labour leaders will be forthcoming. If he had held such discussions, and this is one of the alternatives which the minister was perhaps seeking, it is quite possible that concurrent legislation could have been passed in the
Maritime Transportation Unions United States that might have effectively accomplished the creation of that situation on the great lakes which is the desire of everyone.
I think there is another solution. Everyone seems to have laid the strife on the great lakes at the doorstep of Harold Chamberlain Banks, and I believe rightly so. Everyone I have heard speak in the house on this measure has said it is most regrettable that this legislation must be passed, and everyone who has spoken has left me with the impression that the reason for the legislation is because of the activities of Banks. I should like to pause for a moment to read into the record the official views of the union to which I belong. This is an editorial from the Mine-Mill Herald dated October 1963, written by Mr. Smith, president of the mine-mill union, who writes most of the editorials. He has this to say in an editorial headed: "Both a tragedy and a farce".
The man who said that when history repeats itself it is a tragedy the first time and a farce the second, must now be scratching his head searching for a new definition when he looks at the situation pertaining to Canadian seamen, the Norris report, the antics of Meany and Jodoin, etc., etc.
Let's get what really happened set down and that is no small chore and requires very considerable mental agility to follow the turns and twists of official government and trade union policy.
First, the Canadian seamen had a union of their own that fought to improve their conditions and that had succeeded quite well. Second, under the guise of "anti-communism" the Canadian government, the American state department and the official heads of the trade union movement on both sides of the international border moved everything at hand to smash that union, the C.S.U., and replace it with the goon squad rule of Harold Chamberlain Banks, strong arm convict from the U.S.A. Do-not-ship lists were set up to break the backs of those still sailing who did not agree with these "tender" ministrations and forever keep them off the water. The U.S. state department was happy, the Canadian government was happy,-
May I just pause here to say that I cannot help but think of the exchange which took place when discussing this measure between the Secretary of State and hon. members on this side. I recall the time the Canadian government allowed the entry of Banks into this country, and when the secretary of state for external affairs-I say this without malice at all-had before him the order in council with the record of this man attached to it, a record as long as your arm, he approved his application and allowed the appeal of Banks that he be allowed to stay in this country. I cannot conceive how a thing like that was allowed to happen. Continuing with this editorial:
The U.S. state department was happy, the Canadian government was happy, the shipping companies were happy, Banks was happy.. .everybody was happy except the seamen that had lost their union and their jobs.

Maritime Transportation Unions
Now short years later everybody is unhappy again including the Canadian government that brought Banks here and they are threatening to put his union under a government trusteeship.
Claude Jodoin who helped directly to bring Banks into the country now is making noises that international unions should not interfere in the internal affairs of Canadian unions. We suggest mildly that this is a change because obviously Banks was brought here with Jodoin's assistance for precisely that purpose.
I recall reading a press report concerning Mr. Jodoin, who said of Banks that here is a man who is well on the way to making a good Canadian citizen.
We also recall that a major result of these carrying's on by Jodoin & Co. was the wholesale scuttling of the Canadian merchant marine so that all Canadian shipping became by and large dependant on U.S. bottoms.
At any rate this has all the elements of "tragedy" and "farce" and there can be no solution until the seamen and the workers of Canada proclaim and demand their right to clean up the bloody awful mess. The trickster manoeuvering of a Jodoin who piously now proclaims against the "domination" of U.S. international unions at the behest of the Canadian government that wants to put further shackles on the Canadian unions through their trusteeship, makes nothing but a mess.
The struggle for Canadian independence in general and the struggle specifically for Canadian independence in the trade union movement will grow apace in the days ahead.
As the pioneer international trade union organization that established Canadian autonomy and independence we hail every genuine move in this direction and pledge to stand shoulder to shoulder with anyone who supports that struggle.
We call for an all out offensive by the Canadian workers to put a stop to the farces and the tragedies visited upon them by virtue of the foreign domination of our affairs through the international unions. Canadian workers can do quite well without that, as they can do without the puppet-like capers of Jodoin and his international backers.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder how well the hon. member knows Harvey Murphy. I know Harvey Murphy and have had many discussions with him. Despite the fact that some very poor opinions may have been held about Harvey Murphy owing to his past activities and circumstances, I feel that

Harvey Murphy has been one of the leaders, at least in the north from where I come, in the fight to obtain benefits for the miners in that part of Canada which they would never have received had it not been for Harvey Murphy. I think the parliamentary secretary to the minister will endorse that statement.
I heard that a mine manager from Yellowknife once said of Harvey Murphy at a recent meeting that if it had not been for his presence at that meeting the agreement they were discussing would never have been negotiated.
I should like to quote from the last edition of the Mine-Mill Herald which deals with the address the parliamentary secretary made to the thirteenth convention of the union, and I am sure he will welcome this reference.
-Mr. Byrne did take issue with those who attack the union when he said with reference to the "communist" smear against the union "if the political belief of the members of a union, rather than its accomplishments on behalf of its membership, are to be the criteria upon which the right to existence is judged, then there would be many strange and varied statutes drawn up throughout Canada... the former prime minister's civil rights act would be nothing but a mockery."
I agree 100 per cent with the sentiments expressed there by the parliamentary secretary.
Since everyone seems to have at the back of their minds the elimination of Banks as the cancerous growth at the root of all the strife on the great lakes, I was going to advance another possible alternative, which is action along these lines. The preamble to the bill says that the reason for its passage is because we are confronted with a national emergency, owing to the economic havoc being wrought by the lack of peace on the great lakes. If we are, indeed, confronted with a national emergency, is there not some other method of dealing with the situation? Could we not take action along the same lines as the action we might take in dealing with an emergency at a time when this country was actually involved in a war-and, in effect, this is what is taking place on the great lakes now. If I understand the legal position correctly, Banks is a landed immigrant, not a Canadian citizen. Would it not be possible to amend the Citizenship Act by inserting a section providing specifically, if you wish, for the deportation of Banks as an undesirable individual who should not be allowed to remain in Canada? I think it would be possible to do this. True, it would be an extraordinary measure, but then so is the present legislation. It seems to me the government could have amended the Citizenship Act so as to provide that Mr. Banks no longer had the right to remain in Canada. In my view it would be better to have

done this than to have brought in this trusteeship measure which will merely result in the nationalization of the trade unions on the great lakes. If the government would exert its efforts to bring to the seamen realization that, once Banks had been removed, they would be responsible for electing new officials-strong men imbued with the democratic spirit of free trade unions-we might have been better off than we are as a result of the introduction of the legislation now proposed.
Everybody has had a crack at the shipping companies. If we intend to nationalize the unions, to impose a trusteeship, to take over, in effect, the assets and property of the unions, including their power to make promissory notes and so on, why do we not nationalize the shipping companies as well?

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MARITIME TRANSPORTATION UNIONS
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Everybody is blaming the shipping companies for their part in this affair. It has been said that they and Mr. Jodoin, together with the government, were those responsible for bringing Banks into Canada under the guise of anti-communism. If we intend to press an extraordinary measure of this kind on the trade unions, why not impose a similar one on the shipping companies? What assurance have we now that the shipping companies will fall into line with the wishes of the government? From what I have heard of the representations made by Mr. Leitch, there is no assurance of his co-operation. Maybe the minister has received certain assurances. I do not know.
The last thing the government should do, in my opinion, is to usurp the right of a trade union to manage its own affairs. That is what is now being done. I agree, as do all other hon. members, that Banks should go. If there is no method of prosecuting him and putting him in jail, then, surely, the procedure of amending the Citizenship Act, along the lines I have suggested, would provide a means of kicking him out. This course should have been considered, rather than a measure such as we have before us now-legislation which, in effect, takes the power of managing their own affairs away from the seamen and workers who make up these trade unions.
I do not think the government should have considered interfering with the rights and freedom of a trade union. I do not think they should have considered imposing trustees to manage the affairs of a trade union, any more than they should have thought of imposing a trusteeship over the shipping companies. I want to make that clear, in case anyone misunderstood the analogy I made a few moments ago and which some hon. members on my far left applauded. I do not stand for the nationalization of private enterprise, nor
Maritime Transportation Unions do I stand for the nationalization of trade unions, and I am surprised that members of the New Democratic party should have voted for this measure; because that is precisely what they are supporting-the nationalization of a trade union. If their belief in nationalization extends as far as the nationalization of trade unions, I think they have some soul searching to do.
This legislation has yet another objectionable feature. When the government made known its intention to establish a trusteeship over these maritime unions I had a decision to make and I had great difficulty in reaching the decision which I expressed by my vote today. But when the government spoke of establishing a trusteeship at that time, they talked of doing so on a temporary basis. Now we see that the trusteeship has a five year term to it. Granted, there are provisions in the bill which allow for the ending of the trusteeship, and the handing back of the property taken over, at the end of a period shorter than five years. But to be consistent in its thinking, in accordance with its stated intention to impose the trusteeship on a temporary basis only, I think provision should have been made for supervision on the basis of six months or one year, renewable if necessary. It does not seem to me that it is going to take five years to accomplish the objectives the government has in mind.
There are other objectionable features in this bill. For example, there is the provision which allows the trustees appointed by the government to delegate all their powers to one of their number. Who is to say that if they exercise this power they may not choose another Banks? It seems to me this provision is both dangerous and unwise.
Almost two pages of this bill as it appears before us deal with property and civil rights. It seems to me that to allow a trusteeship to take over the assets and property which belong to the members of a trade union is completely unacceptable. It is an action which sets an extremely dangerous precedent and, for these reasons, this is a measure which I cannot in all conscience bring myself to support. I feel the situation should have been handled by dethroning Banks by other means and I have yet to be convinced that this could not be done. One of the aims of the government should have been to explore the possibility to the full of Canadianizing the Canadian portion of this union, before introducing such legislation as we have before us. The management of trade unions must be left to the membership of those unions and it seems to me to be completely wrong in principle to introduce a measure such as this trusteeship proposal which takes away a fundamental right of workers in Canada in

Maritime Transportation Unions any section of the economy to organize themselves into trade unions. This, in my opinion, is the first step toward eroding the functions of trade unionism, a principle in which I believe as being necessary to our Canadian way of life.
I do hope that perhaps some explanation or some comment will be forthcoming from the minister on the solution which I have suggested in connection with the amendment to the Citizenship Act to enable us to deport Mr. Banks, rather than ask for this extraordinary step to be taken.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I suggest that the problem necessitating this legislation is a generic problem of our Canadian-United States relations. It is one of the results of this nation having been conceived as an entity which would stretch from east to west, while the lines of nature and basic economics envisage a flow from north to south. Its roots are in the same vein which periodically give birth to the outcry about United States capital control of our industry and of our heritage. When the problem relates to economic entities such as trade unions, which in one land are regarded in the perspective of persons geared to the republican form of government while in the other land the same economic entity, the trade union, is geared by those who are brought up in the background of parliamentary government, then the problem of that fundamental contradiction in our Canadian conception becomes more acute.
When Mr. Wirtz and Mr. Meany rail at us, they do so as the products of the republican system of checks and balances, pressure against pressure, which regards overt governmental interference as virtually sacrilegious, while pressures, governmental or otherwise, are the order of the day. When, on the other hand, we recoil from such pressure with righteous and jingoistic indignation, we quite properly do so as the children of a parliamentary democracy, where parliament is supreme and any outside pressure on parliament is an invasion of our most profound and sacred rights. In all areas of such difference, Mr. Chairman, which I suggest will ever recur as economic necessity brings us closer to our neighbours to the south, I think the road to progress will surely be in the nonflashy but reliable car of moderation.
On the one hand, we should develop our ability to think as republicans while they, on the other hand, should develop their ability to think as parliamentarians. I think this is preferable to the lofty and futile high horse. During this twenty sixth parliament, Mr. Chairman, we have heard often and loud

the voice of faction, the voice of colloquialism, the voice of provincialism. How still and small and seldom heard has been the voice of Canada. Here we have a great, and I believe, transcendent problem which may well affect all Canada and all Canadians. It is, perhaps, the way of democracy that when the problem is so grave as to affect all of Canada and all Canadians, the debate in this house has been on a higher plane, more loftily and properly conducted in the national interest and in the highest parliamentary tradition, than has been the case with any measure which has been brought before this twenty sixth parliament.
I think I should say also, Mr. Chairman, that the party to which I belong, this house and, yes, the whole nation, is indebted to the minister who has sponsored this bill. In his conduct of this matter he has established for himself an enviable, an unassailable position for efficiency, patience and courtesy in the manner in which he has handled this difficult and trying problem from its inception. It has been recently stated in the press that we in the backbenches of this party have some fault, or had some fault to find with the frontbenchers of this party. I can only say that we who sit back here with our posteriors on the edge of the Ottawa river are very proud of the way in which the minister has handled this matter. We have been very pleased to sit behind him. I can only say, Mr. Chairman, it is to be hoped that this house will continue in the manner and spirit which has prevailed in the debate on this measure, so that it may be said of the twenty sixth parliament that it was a bit of a shambles until the debate on the trusteeship bill, but from that time forward matters were handled in the house in the parliamentary manner, and on the highest basis.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING COUNT OF VOTES AT ADVANCE POLLS
AMENDMENT RESPECTING COUNT OF VOTES AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. C-26, to amend the Canada Elections Act (advance polls).

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING COUNT OF VOTES AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to amend the Canada Elections Act in order to prevent a repetition in the next election or in subsequent ones of offences or irregularities such as those committed in the last election in my riding, as well as in other constituencies in Canada.
I know that all members of the house are quite familiar with the Canada Elections Act and are aware that it was amended in 1960 in order to increase the number of advance polls in various electoral districts.


Those advance polls are open on the ninth day and the seventh day prior to the day of the election so that people who expect to be absent from their country or electoral district on election day may have a chance to vote.
I believe that amendment has given many electors the opportunity of exercising their franchise before the date of the election. However, infractions can be committed in those advance polls. I know that, at the last election, in my riding, a deputy returning officer counted the ballots at the end of the first day of voting at the advance polls. Results in one advance poll were made known. I realized then that if the act was not amended, that could have serious effects in certain constituencies, especially when the electors know how the voting went a week or nine days before election day.
If results at some advance polls are revealed prematurely, that can have a great influence on the vote on election day.
That is why I propose this amendment. Besides, the hon. members know that the deputy returning officer is responsible for the ballot box at the advance poll on voting day and keeps it in his possession until the actual voting day. And it is only in the evening of that day, two hours after the closing of the polls, that the deputy returning officer, in the presence of representatives of the various candidates, must open the ballot box of the advance poll.
The present act is not sufficiently strict with regard to offences committed by the deputy returning officer when he is caught doing something illegal, as happened in my riding.
As a matter of fact, the only punishment that can be meted out to him is that he loses one day's salary or his salary for the two days he worked at the poll as deputy returning officer.
Therefore, there is a serious danger, because at a given time one or several deputy returning officers could conspire with various organizers to count the votes in a number of advance polls so as to publish the results before election day.
Under the Canada Elections Act, anyone guilty of divulging prematurely the results of the voting at a poll is liable to a fine ranging from $1 to $500.
In my opinion, our aim would be achieved by this amendment if a deputy returning officer who counts the ballots before election day were liable to the same penalty as any person who publishes the results of the election ahead of time and were fined from $1 to $500.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to support the measure which was presented by our colleague, the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc). I do not intend to spend too much time on this, but I should like to explain my views on that subject.
My riding is the third largest in Canada; it is outranked only by Scarborough and Mercier. Over 60,000 of my constituents are residents of the northern part of Montreal and another 58,000 live on Jesus island where eight cities and five towns are located.
During the June 1962 election, the chief electoral officer set up 22 advanced polls and many Canadians took advantage of the right they had under the Canada Elections Act, to vote before the official date of the election.
Now, it just happened that in four advanced polls, the returning officer announced the results in favour of one of my opponents with the consequence that, because of the indiscretion committed by the officials, on voting day, the vote was next to nothing in the district where those polls were situated.
I quite understand that, as my colleague for Gatineau has just explained, under the present legislation, a deputy returning officer who commits an indiscretion loses his job and is not entitled to any pay. However, as my hon. friend said, that is not enough and if such a returning officer has to pay a $500 fine just like any person who publishes prematurely the election results, people would think twice before acting and I am convinced that in the case I am concerned with at present, things would have been different.
In a riding such as mine, Mr. Speaker, with more than 118,000 voters, even if the vote is thus switched around a bit, the effects are not as far reaching as they would be in a smaller constituency, as the hon. member for Gatineau pointed out a moment ago, where that could be enough to alter the results completely and bring about a vote which would be the reverse of the opinion the electors would otherwise have expressed.
I am sure all of us in this house, Mr. Speaker, no matter which party we belong to, want truly democratic and honest elections, and I know this bill would be suited to that purpose and would prevent many mistakes being made.
Sometimes, Mr. Speaker, caught in the election turmoil, we ourselves, members of our organization, the returning officer and his assistants, unfortunately cannot prevent some thoughtless campaign officials from doing such things. They do things such as the
It rests with us, members of this house, to prevent such situations and, without prejudice, under our oath of office, to legislate so as to assure not only the integrity of the administration, but also that of those who will be called upon later on, as ourselves, to govern the country.
It remains with the hon. members, Mr. Speaker, to protect the public against itself, to protect certain organizers, whatever party they belong to, against the extravagant enthusiasm they show during an election campaign in favour of a candidate of their choice.
The bill of our colleague for Gatineau has been introduced for no other purpose than to assure the honesty of the vote and to give to the people members of their choice. In other words, it is a matter of electing a truly democratic government, fully representative of a common ideal.
Mr. Speaker, these are troubled times in which we live. Let us be on our guard, for tomorrow may be too late. Those who live under a democratic government tend to forget that elsewhere things may be different. Although dictators are clever at painting things a lovely rosy hue, their subjects become tools in the hands of a small group of men, of potentates who, in the name of the nation, use them as mere puppets to satisfy the mad ambitions of vainglorious masters thirsting for power.
That fact is illustrated by the story of the last 20 years. Nazi Germany and fascist Italy dreamt of holding sway over a trembling world and, in fact, succeeded in enslaving whole nations, but they have since paid a bitter price, and drunk to the dregs the cup of humiliation. Hitler committed suicide in his lair in the Bavarian Alps and Mussolini was delivered to public obloquy and hanged, as we know, by his feet.
It will be objected that the situation is not quite so bad. I agree. But in the last five years, even in the last two or three years, the difficulties which have occurred on all sides are different from those of the past.
People luxuriate in liberty and quite properly demand that their rights be respected, placing on our shoulders heavier responsibilities which are quite different from those of the past due to the needs of our times.
This bill, Mr. Speaker, as modest as it is, if we stop and consider it carefully, will remedy many mistakes and particularly many unfortunate abuses of the past.

Canada Elections Act
That is why, on behalf of the voters in my riding, I make it my duty to support this measure introduced by our colleague from Gatineau.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will take a few minutes only to express my views about the measure under consideration.
First of all, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Montreal-Laval (Mr. Rochon) for the sincerity with which he supported the bill introduced by the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc), but I must tell him that I do not share his view about advance polls set up when a general election is held.
Such advance polls are set up to give the greatest number of electors the opportunity to cast their votes before the date set for the election, when they have to be away on voting day.
If my memory is correct, I think those advance polls have been used only in the last two general elections. Previously, those advance polls were open only one day.
During the 1962 and 1963 elections, the polls were open, as the hon. member for Gatineau pointed out, the ninth day and the seventh day before election day.
I feel that this measure was presented to the house following the mistakes that were made across Canada during the last general election, but I think that if you compare the few mistakes made with the number of polls set up for the 1963 election, you realize that the number of deputy returning officers who made such mistakes was negligible and just because a few deputy returning officers made mistakes, I do not feel that we should necessarily amend the act and go back to the years when advance polls were opened just for one day.
Mr. Speaker, I have here the result of the voting in the four last federal elections for my riding. If we consider the number of voters who cast their vote at advance polls, we readily realize that those polls have certainly enabled a great many Canadians to exercise their franchise, compared to previous years.
In 1957, for instance, 11 voters reported to the advance poll in St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, whereas only ten did in 1958. But if we study the results of the 1962 general election, we find that the number has gone up to the extent that 101 voters exercised their franchise, and this, because the advance poll remained open for two days instead of one.
Mr. Speaker, the previous speakers tried to influence our judgment, but I do not think there is much danger of being misled by their contentions.

For instance, the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc) claimed that the results could be known prematurely under the present procedure. Besides, he mentioned that the scrutiny of the votes cannot be made, by virtue of the act, before two hours after the closing of the polls.
Well, if the object of this bill is to punish those who are bent on transgressing the law,
I am afraid that the hon. member's efforts will be in vain.
In my opinion, the important thing is to try and teach people who hold offices in polls to act only according to the law.
In fact, I think that most of the mistakes made are due to ignorance rather than ill will.
In the last election, the result of the voting in an advance poll in my riding was published before the national voting day, and I am convinced that that mistake was not made through ill will.
And how can the rest of voters in the riding be influenced by that, since only five or six voters go to an advance poll?
And even if all votes had been for one candidate or the other, that certainly does not represent the general opinion and would not influence at all the rest of the voters in that constituency to vote in favour of such or such candidate in particular.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that instead of passing the measure now before us, we should, in a general election, give the necessary instructions to those who are entrusted with the duties of deputy returning officers. Briefly, instead of changing the present provisions which enable more voters to use their right to vote, we should rather make allowance for the advantages granted to the voters under the present legislation.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING COUNT OF VOTES AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have but brief comments to make about Bill C-26. I am happy to see that the hon. member for Gatineau (Mr. Leduc) has brought in this bill to amend in parts the Canada Elections Act particularly, as far as the advance polls are concerned.
The hon. member for Laval (Mr. Rochon) said a moment ago that such an amendment to the election act might forestall the advent of a totalitarian state in Canada. Personally, I feel that my hon. friend got carried away, and that his words went beyond his thoughts. We must admit that nazism in Germany and the totalitarian regime in Italy were bred by factors much more vital than those we are striving to rectify through this piece of legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I endorse the remarks of the hon. member who sponsored the bill and I wish to quote a case which occurred in my

own riding during the 1962 general election.
An advanced poll had been established in the town of Roxton Falls and about 15 persons having the same political views had been allowed to vote. After the closing of the poll, it was learned that the result of the vote had been made public not only in many neighbouring parishes but also in the main centres, especially the town of Granby.
That indiscretion surely influenced the voters. In fact, I received many telephone calls on that matter. I was also informed about it by political organizations. Also, the returning officer in my riding had to make a statement over the radio to the effect that the results were not official.
Therefore, I think it is wise to bring forward such a piece of legislation.
I do not deny that abuses might still take place but if the act is not amended, similar errors might be repeated.
Everyone knows that those who have a thorough knowledge of the Elections Act can take advantage of certain circumstances. It was also said that the errors disclosed were due to ignorance. It might be true in most cases-at least, I trust it is-but I am convinced that as far as I am concerned, what happened in 1962 was certainly not due to ignorance, but was well premeditated because the whole thing had been planned. Fortunately, the damage done in that community could be repaired because the necessary action was taken.
Mr. Speaker, I will not labour the point in order not to hold up the passing of Bill C-26 so that the nation can have a better elections act in the future.

Mr. Reid Scot! (Danforlh): I just want to make one or two comments on the proposal before the house. It is not that I object to the principle of the bill; I think there is some merit in the proposal itself. But I should like to say a word in defence of the deputy returning officers. No doubt, conditions vary from one riding to another. I do not pretend to know much about electoral procedure in the riding of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, but we have found that most of the deputy returning officers are sincere people. They are not particularly well schooled in their duties or activities and I think most of the mistakes they make arise, not through malice on their part, but largely through indifference, or ignorance of their duties. In these circumstances I doubt that it is very wise to impose penalties of the type envisaged in this bill.
I presume, of course, that the measure would be referred to the committee on privileges and elections so that it could be studied
Canada Elections Act
in greater detail and its terms debated, but I think it would be unwise to pass a blanket provision imposing penalties on these people. Perhaps the penalty should only be imposed if some serious malice can be shown or some intent to influence the decision of the electorate. There should be some safeguard in the bill so that innocent people will not bear this onerous penalty.
There are, of course, many matters in connection with elections which should be dealt with in the privileges and elections committee. Certainly, we should do something about prohibiting the publication of public opinion polls during the course of an election. These have, sometimes, an unusual appeal to the population, and perhaps consideration of this matter might be included. At the same time, something should be done about preventing United States stations from broadcasting eastern results in western Canada before the polls close. This, again, would seem to be an infringement of our rights. These are matters which, perhaps, could be studied by the committee.
I hope the hon. gentleman's bill will be referred to the committee because, as I have indicated, we approve of the general principle. We feel that the abuse the hon. member is trying to correct is one which should be corrected. However, we do not want to see a lot of innocent deputy returning officers penalized for mistakes which they are only making out of a lack of knowledge or, more likely, a lack of instruction from the returning officer. I am not criticizing returning officers. They have too much to do in a short time, and it is not always possible to correctly school the deputy returning officers. All this might be corrected if we could institute a permanent voters list, and permanent deputy returning officers who would be in touch with their polls. Perhaps these are matters that could be gone into by the committee. I thought that someone from our party should indicate that there was merit in the hon. member's suggestion, and the measure should go to committee where it could receive the fair treatment it obviously merits.

When I look at the clock, Mr. Speaker, I am reminded that I can only speak briefly in support of this measure. I would point out to the house that, as the law now stands, there is an absolute prohibition against the publication of the results in any newspaper. There is nothing said about whether the newspaper does this with malice or otherwise.

Maritime Transportation Unions As long as the newspaper publishes the information, then it is liable to a fine or imprisonment. I do not know how you imprison a newspaper, but I suppose you can imprison the executives.
In so far as the deputy returning officers are concerned, they can only be fined or imprisoned under section 97 if it can be shown that they acted in a corrupt manner. This is a very difficult thing, of course, to prove. It is my feeling that there should be teeth put into this elections act so that the deputy returning officer will be liable to an automatic fine and/or imprisonment. Now, this may seem very harsh, Mr. Speaker, but the purpose is to prevent an unscrupulous group getting together in several ridings spread throughout the country. Then, the day preceding the actual election day, they could get as many of their supporters as possible to the advance polls and make arrangements to ensure that the results of four or five of these advance polls are leaked to the public.
I am not suggesting this would be done, but it could be done. If it were done, then we create this band-wagon approach to an election. We know that a good many of our neighbours vote a certain way because their neighbours are voting a certain way. They do not necessarily vote on the merits of the situation, but they jump on the band-wagon. I would urge that teeth be put into the law. I agree with the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) that when these results are made known in advance by the deputy returning officer, it is generally out of curiosity and there is no malice entailed. However, there is a danger of this happening. I see the hour is late, and I understand the measure is going to be referred to the committee on privileges and elections, so I will conclude my remarks.

I feel it is quite possible some rather serious errors were made at that time in dealing with the situation that then prevailed, but now we should face up to the realities of the present situation. What may or may not have been done, correctly or incorrectly, in connection with that situation is almost a matter of ancient history and should not be of primary concern now to either members of trade unions in Canada or members of this committee.
The thing I most vividly remember about that situation is my feeling at the time that much of what was done then was done because of certain pressures which were exerted upon the government of Canada and the Canadian trade union movement by those who live in the country to the south of us; and in view of the pride which the hon. member for Yukon indicated in the fact that the union of which he is a member has taken a strong Canadian union position, I find it rather difficult to comprehend his apparent lack of readiness to object to the kind of pressures that are being exerted in the current situation in Canada.
When he spoke earlier on second reading my colleague, the hon. member for Port Arthur, suggested that this really was not the time for us to be indulging in recriminations or reminiscences concerning the past history of the situation which led up to the mess in which we are at present, and I feel that should be the basic point from which we should approach this legislation. I also feel the hon. member for Yukon was putting the gloomiest possible construction upon the things that might happen as a result of the passage of this bill.
I think he would agree that no hon. member who has spoken so far has suggested this is a desirable step, but rather it would appear that what has happened in the past makes it the only possible step we can take. So far

as I am concerned I am at once willing to concede I fully expect a great many difficulties will arise consequent upon the passage of the bill. We would be blind to the realities of the situation if we did not recognize that fact but I also feel we have a responsibility, particularly those of us who are reluctantly prepared to agree to the passage of the bill, to watch very carefully over the manner in which it is put into operation. We have a responsibility from time to time, if we consider it justified, to be critical of the manner in which the trusteeship is operated, but we also have a responsibility to do our best to see that it functions successfully.
As I see it, of course, the first requirement has to do with the calibre and experience of the trustees who are chosen. I am sure the Minister of Labour is not unaware of the importance of that matter, and I hope he is going to be able to find people to assume this responsibility who, because of their personality, their character and their knowledge will be able from the start to give proper prestige to this body and will be able to bring the right kind of wisdom to bear.
My prime purpose in trying to catch your eye originally, Mr. Chairman, prior to when the hon. member for the Yukon spoke, was to come back to the matter raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North, namely, what the intentions of the government are, if any, with respect to dealing with the shipping companies referred to in the Norris commission report. I feel that the Minister of Labour, in view of the fact he is piloting this bill, should give us some indication of his thinking in this matter and what the intentions, if any, of the government are in this connection.
I can understand that the Minister of Labour may be somewhat reluctant to do this, and in a sense I would agree it is not primarily his responsibility because, in my view, the particular bill before us has to do with the union aspect of the situation and is of direct interest and concern to him as Minister of Labour. I would assume that any steps which might be taken to correct some of the wrongdoings that have gone on, on the company side of the picture, would not necessarily fall directly under the responsibility of the Minister of Labour, or that any proposals which might be brought before parliament by the government would not necessarily be brought forward in his name.
Actually, I believe the person who should rise in the house during the course of this discussion and make a statement as to the government's intentions is the head of the government, the Prime Minister, because in
Maritime Transportation Unions my opinion this is a matter of the broad policy of the present administration which I think could properly be dealt with by the Prime Minister, either in this debate or outside it. In any event, before clause 1 of the bill carries I hope the Minister of Labour, as the spokesman of the government at this time, will indicate to us in no uncertain terms just what the intentions of the government are in connection with any action that may be proposed, to ensure that the companies involved are going to become respectable, law-abiding Canadian companies.
