Mr. Chairman, I opposed a trusteeship, and because a few others who have opposed it have stated their reasons may I say that I certainly do not want to be associated with the reasons advanced by former speakers in this debate. I, too, remember the day of Pat Sullivan and the old Canadian seamen's union. It was felt that the action taken then was in the best interests of the trade union movement, and it is unfortunate that history has not proven this to be correct.
However, the arguments that have been used as a basis for opposing the bill do not necessarily represent my objections. I think I can state my objections fairly simply. First, I have an inherent dislike for trusteeship. I think this is shared by almost every trade unionist in Canada and throughout the world. I am sure this view is shared by most members of parliament and in particular by the Minister of Labour himself. I also think that the dislike is even greater when trusteeship is applied in a legislative way, because it takes away from the workers any rights in the foreseeable future with regard to the operation of their own organization.
I am only guessing and can only guess, but I presume that a man who has been sitting in the gallery today may be one of the trustees. I hope this is true, because I can remember when I was more or less under trusteeship as a member of a union that was under discussion in another sense this afternoon. I can remember this gentleman coming to the mining area. He was highly acceptable to that area and he gave encouragement to the people and helped to establish a democratically based union there. I hope that history may repeat itself and that his success may be as great in this instance. It might be said that there was almost a trusteeship that time, under the congress of that day; but at no time was it ever suggested that this was something to be desired or welcomed, but rather that it was something to be used only because there did not seem to be any other relief. The same problem is repeating itself and making it necessary for

Maritime Transportation Unions intervention from without, in view of the fact that the constitution and machinery-available to the workers is not such as to allow them to do something for themselves.
My second reason is a very simple one. I hope very strongly that I am wrong in my views, because if I am not the situation will be chaotic. It is my expectation that the trusteeship will not do what it is intended to do. It would seem that all Canadians have decided that the remedy to clean up the S.I.U. must be the removal of Mr. Banks. This can be accomplished, of course, because of the illegal acts that have been committed in the past, but yet nobody seems to be sure that there will be any legal arrangement made to dispose of Mr. Banks.
I believe the minister has said on a number of occasions that under the circumstances this gentleman cannot be deported. I find this is quite true. A landed immigrant can never be deported unless the country from which he came or to which we wish to deport him is willing to accept him, and under the circumstances this may be very difficult to accomplish. This may be one bad apple we will have a heck of a time giving away. We do not want him and probably nobody else does. I hope I am wrong, but I am wondering whether there is any chance for the trusteeship to accomplish what we hope it will.
As for my third reason, I would point out that this situation has already had one very good result. From this less than desirable situation there has developed a Canadianism that has been sadly lacking in this House of Commons for a long time. We have become more used to separatism and division on our national scene than we have to unity of national purpose. It has even brought many of the members of the House of Commons together in this matter. If this is an accomplishment that has been achieved, everything will not be wasted, if we are able to develop a sense of responsible nationalism in Canada, pointing out to some other people some of the faults that have no doubt existed in the past and honestly paying some tribute to some of the advantages that have accrued to the Canadian people because of the exercise of responsibilities and duties of people outside our own country.
I only wanted to make it very clear that my reasons for opposing this were not necessarily the same as others who have opposed it. I do so, knowing full well that we have no alternative to offer, and I know that an alternative or some solution to the problem must be arrived at. I hope that some of the changes that may make it more acceptable will be introduced by the government during the passage of this legislation. If that is done,


this measure will, in my opinion, have more chance of success than it appears to have with its present terms.

I realize it is not necessarily within the jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour, but it would be most helpful if, before allowing clause 1 to carry, we could have a statement from the minister or somebody on the government side indicating that the other culprits to the conspiracy, namely the shipping companies, are not going to be permitted to get off scot free in this matter.
We are not suggesting necessarily that they should be placed under trusteeship also. I am not sure that this is practical. But we would like some indication as to what proposals the government may have in mind or what action it intends to take to see that the other parties to this whole conspiracy are also given some attention. I do not want to belabour all the evidence that has gone on the record. Other hon. members on this side of the chamber have read into the record the incontrovertible evidence of the collusion that took place between the S.I.U. and the various shipping companies, collusion in violation of the laws of Canada. Without this collusion much of the trouble could not have happened. We would like at this stage, Mr. Chairman, before clause 1 is carried, to have some indication from the government as to what measures they may have in mind to deal with the other guilty parties to this disgraceful conspiracy against the laws of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, my comments will be very brief. This whole subject has been given a very excellent debate in this house, and I would just like to stress a few points. This whole situation with which we are faced today seems to be one long

retreat from a series of evils. If we go back far enough we find it was the evil of the shipping companies that first led to the communist dominated union on the great lakes. Then to get rid of the evil of this communist domination we brought in the evil of Hal Banks; and when that evil becomes more than we could stomach we bring in the evil of this trusteeship. Let us not forget; it is an evil. I think we all do, or should, recognize this. Surely history has taught us that evils do not correct themselves; somebody must make some move some place along the line to correct them. I think this is something that should remain in the minds of hon. members of this house. We are now faced with two evils, the evil of this legislation that we have to pass to cure a worse evil, and we still have with us-as has been pointed out by many hon. members-the original evil that started it all off, as represented by the shipping companies which have been hand in glove with Hal Banks over the years. Therefore this legislation has the support of the house to cure one particular evil; but let us not forget that there is another one to be corrected. Let us not leave this evil too long on the books.

Mr. Chairman, in 1834 we had the tremendous case of the Tolpuddle martyrs
Maritime Transportation Unions who were prosecuted by the government of the day because they formed an association of free men in the form of a trade union. I consider it a sorry state of affairs that in 1963, in the Dominion of Canada, we are passing legislation which brings under government trusteeship associations of free men. I wonder how many members of the Canadian House of Commons realize that of the six martyrs of Tolpuddle of 1834, all of whom were transported to Australia by an unjust decree and an unfair government, five, after they left Australia, emigrated to Canada and lie buried in the province of Ontario. Those five Tolpuddle martyrs who suffered grievous injury and wrong because of their beliefs that free men should be allowed to freely associate in a trade union lie in western Ontario, in cemeteries in the vicinity of London, Byron and St. Marys. It is interesting to note that one martyr of Tolpuddle, who lived the longest, to the age of 92, lies buried today in St. Marys, Ontario, in the same cemetery as a former prime minister of the Dominion of Canada.
In justifying my action in supporting this measure brought in by the government that I support, I would point out that when Liberal candidates ran in 1962 and again in 1963, we were assured by our leader that we had tremendous messes to clean up resulting from the inefficiency and indolence of the government that was then on its way out. When I stood for parliament in 1962, I did so knowing that this country was faced with a crisis resulting from the inability of the then government to handle the affairs of the nation. I tell you that the messes facing the present government of the Right Hon. Lester Pearson make the 12 labours of Hercules a mere myth. One of the tasks of Hercules was to clean the Augean stables. The Augeans thought he would refuse because he could not stand the stench of the offal and refuse around the cattle barns of the estates. We Liberal candidates in 1962 knew the refuse and offal that was lying around the cattle barns of the government. We volunteered to clean up the mess.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was going to draw an analogy between the fact that Hercules diverted two rivers into the Augean stables to clean up the mess and this action

Maritime Transportation Unions of the government's, on the St. Lawrence seaway, which will clear up the situation which has developed there.
I	should like to draw to the attention of the committee, because I have not heard any other speaker refer to it, the fact that on page 298 of the Norris report you will find this sentence which goes to the heart of the entire report. Mr. Justice Norris writes:
II	any one thing was demonstrated on this inquiry, it was how lawlessness (including in the term disregard of the rule of law, of constituted authority, and of contractual obligations) begets lawlessness.
Mr. Justice Norris says that if any one thing was demonstrated in this inquiry it was how lawlessness begets lawlessness. I regret that in the clouds of hysteria surrounding this matter many have intimated that the lawlessness was on the part of one union led by one man. If hon. members would read the Norris report, and I regret exceedingly the large number of members who have not read the Norris report, they would find he attacks the shipping companies as well as the trade union on this matter of lawlessness. At page 298 of the report, Mr. Justice Norris adds this:
It was at any time within the power of the C.S.L. with all its strength and influence to accomplish much in stabilizing the great lakes situation by taking a positive stand on the side of law and order, but for the sake of a present- at best uneasy-peace and for competitive advantage, it not only did nothing, but gave support to Banks, the lawbreaker. It showed a cynical disregard for its contractual obligations with the N.A.M.E.
Now, the Norris report points out that Canada Steamship Lines is the biggest of the Canadian companies, and its actions were generally followed by the other companies. The C.S.L. was the bellwether of the flock.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North read into the record the other day a list of the directors of the Canada Steamship Lines. The Secretary of State, in reply to a question, has read into the record the names of the directors of Misener steamships. Anyone who is acquainted with business life in Canada knows that these men are the leaders of our business community today. I came into the house at the age of 60, after 40 years in the business world. I would not have anyone think that I consider the members of the Canadian cabinet to be the ablest men of their age and generation. The members of Canadian cabinets have a job to do and most members do it well.
However, there are businessmen in this country who, immediately an election has taken place, begin to size up those people selected for the cabinet. I can assure you that following the elections of 1957 and 1958 the businessmen of this country sized up the

members of the cabinet, took their measure and knew exactly how far they could go with whatever endeavour they wished to carry out.
Now, the record concerning the disregard of one of the shipping companies for the law of the land has been brought to our attention, and reference has been made to it in the Norris report on pages 54 and 55. I do not need to read the record again. However, I would point out that not only had the steamship directors a cynical disregard for the Minister of Labour, but even the Canadian brotherhood of railway and transport workers expressed their opinion of the ability of the previous government. On page 14 of the Norris report we find some extracts of the evidence given by Mr. Frederick Nicoll, director of organizing and servicing for the Canadian brotherhood of railway, transport and general workers. Under questioning, Mr. Nicoll was asked what he hoped to accomplish by the boycott that was called on vessels passing through the St. Lawrence seaway and the Welland canal. His reply was as follows:
We hope to accomplish two things. Mr. Wright. Basically-primarily, rather; one was to force the situation where the Canadian manned ships that were presently being boycotted in the United States would be released from the boycott and we were hopeful that we were going to jockey the Canadian government into taking these steps which had been suggested by ourselves for I don't know how many years, by the Canadian Labour Congress in 1962, that there should be an industrial inquiry commission established to go into the whole sad sorry mess-
Q. Yes, and in retrospect did you accomplish- not did you accomplish, but were these two objectives accomplished?
A. As far as we are concerned, yes.
Mr. Nicoll is saying that the Canadian brotherhood of railway and transport workers jockeyed the Canadian government into the position that they desired. Now, a jockey rides an animal and is in control of that animal. He can make him go wherever the jockey wishes him to go. I ask, does this sound like a strong, independent government when an official of a brotherhood stands up and says they were hopeful they would jockey the Canadian government? In answer to a direct question he said they accomplished their purpose.
Now, the steamship lines wrote a letter to Mr. Bernard Wilson, the director of industrial relations, a very enlightening and revealing letter. In the course of the letter to Mr. Wilson, Misener Steamship Lines under date of April 10, 1959, stated that they realized their course of action was against the labour relations act. This letter came to the Department of Labour of the federal

government. Along with that letter, Mr. Wilson received a copy of a letter of indemnification granted by the seamen's international union to the Misener Steamship Lines. Mr. Justice Norris made the comment that similar letters were sent to other shipping companies. I say to you that the federal government was notified by letter under date of April 10, 1959, that these steamship companies were breaking the law, and the government did absolutely nothing about it. The letter stated frankly that this course was against the labour relations act.
We on this side of the house have been trying to explain the inaction of the government during the five and a half years it was in power. Many of us thought that friendships with directors of some of the big steamship companies were responsible for the inaction and indolence which characterized the former government, particularly so far as the Department of Labour was concerned. However, I have a good friend of 40 years standing who is a director of a steamship company, and I could not believe that he would stoop to such a practice. And lo and behold, this is what the former minister of labour told us, not only last night between a quarter to ten and ten, but also the day before, as reported on page 3432 of Hansard:
As I pointed out yesterday, any initiative on the part of the government to launch an inquiry into the affairs of a union which was affiliated with the Canadian Labour Congress would have aroused the most terrible attack upon the government by all members of the Canadian Labour Congress.
I want to repeat that to hon. members for emphasis.

The former minister of labour said:
-any initiative on the part of the government to launch an inquiry into the affairs of a union which was affiliated with the Canadian Labour Congress would have aroused the most terrible attack upon the government by all members of the Canadian Labour Congress.
But the former minister of labour did not point out that in June, 1959, the Canadian Labour Congress had kicked the S.I.U. out of the Canadian Labour Congress. So that means that from June, 1959, until the government resigned in April of this year, a period of three years and ten months, the S.I.U. was not affiliated with the Canadian Labour Congress; so the reason advanced by the former minister falls to the ground.
If you look at the supplements to the Norris report and at schedule 31 you will find listed there by Mr. Justice Norris examples of intimidation and violence. Nineteen cases of beatings are listed. No action was taken
Maritime Transportation Unions on those 19 cases which Mr. Justice Norris listed as occurring between August 18, 1957, when the former government was in power, and August 20, 1962. I should like to point out that of the 19 cases of beatings only the first two cases occurred when the S.I.U. was an affiliate of the C.L.C. The remaining 17 cases took place after the C.L.C. had rejected the S.I.U. as a member of their organization.
The hon. member for Ontario stated last night that when the record of lawlessness and malpractice on the great lakes had grown sufficiently serious action should then have been taken by this government. I would point out that the record of beatings and harassment and property damage occurred during the tenure of office of the former minister of labour. He had been properly sized up by the businessmen of this country and they knew how far they could push him. They knew how far they could go and they signed illegal contracts. They then notified him that they had signed them, knowing that in his ineptitude no action would be taken against them. As Mr. Justice Norris said in his report, lawlessness begets lawlessness.
This situation has been forced on this government by the inaction of the previous government, and I thank heaven we now have a government in power which is willing to take action. On page 296 of his report Mr. Justice Norris points out, in his conclusions, referring to Banks, that he and his union operated a vacation pay plan unlawfully and contrary to the directions of the minister of labour. Could anything be more plainly stated than that? Now we have a Minister of Labour who is willing to take action and who has notified the ship owners that they are not to send that vacation pay money to the S.I.U. but that it is to be returned directly to the employees. And in addition, the minister has taken action to recover $300,000 from the
S.I.U. which money Mr. Justice Norris said was being administered unlawfully. What did the former minister of labour do to clean up that situation?
While I have pointed out the ineptitude of the former government and how it has brought us to the situation where we have to take action by legislating the affairs of unions, a step which is against the convictions and lifetime practices of members of the Liberal party, I should also stress that the inaction of the previous government has put a strain on our relations with the United States government. That is to be regretted. Our relations with the world must be based on friendly relations with the United States. Our relations with the United States are now strained, and this situation is going to take very careful

Maritime Transportation Unions handling. This has been forced on the government by the inaction of the previous government. Last night the former minister pointed out that when he was minister of labour the relations between Canada and the United States were such that we would be called bosom pals. Now he says there is a conflict between us. I say there is no fighting in a cemetery. Where there is no action there is no disagreement. But the moment this government, under our present Prime Minister, steps forward to straighten out the situation we receive protests from the United States, and we are told by members of the opposition that we are causing trouble.
In the course of discussion on this bill we have been told time and time again that Mr. Banks is the darling of the Liberal party; that Mr. Banks was brought into Canada by the Liberal party; that Mr. Banks has been nurtured in this country by the Liberal party, and that he expects to receive the same friendship from this government that he received from the St. Laurent government. I ask, Mr. Chairman, how could we extend any more friendship to this man than was extended by the former government, when you read their record of inaction-lack of police court action against the S.I.U. in connection with their activities throughout the country, all of which is documented by Mr. Justice Norris? The statement has been made several times that Mr. Banks has been granted the status of a landed immigrant; that the previous government, again because of their ineptitude examined the law of the land and found that Mr. Banks could not be deported from this country. When this was challenged and it was pointed out that he could be deported if he violated certain laws of the land, we got that hollow laugh that bespeaks the vacant mind and were told no, he could not be deported. According to a press release which appeared in the Toronto daily Star on Monday, September 23, the former prime minister revealed that his government had had Mr. Banks fully investigated, but concluded that it could not deport him because of an order in council. Yesterday the Secretary of State challenged that statement, pointing out that Mr. Banks can be deported if he at any time violates the law of the land, and that he would be deported if he were to do anything that justified such action.
It is a little difficult to follow the comments of some of the speakers so far. I knew a former member for Broadview very well, and I will long remember a comment made by the late Joe Clark, who was father to Gregory and editor of the Toronto daily Star for about 40 years.

After I am through speaking. Mr. Clark referred to the former member for Broadview, Ontario, as being the greatest orator Canada had ever seen because he was entirely unhampered by facts. They gave him the status of a man who was above challenge, so long as thereafter he lived within the law.
That is exactly what we Liberals have been saying. And in the very next sentence the right hon. gentleman goes on to say, entirely unhampered by the facts-"but Banks was above the law". In his first breath he says he was given the status of a man above challenge as long as thereafter he lived within the law-which is correct. And then, in the next sentence he says: "but he was above the law". How is one to believe statements made in this manner? The first statement was accurate. The second was as false as the Secretary of State stated it to be.
I regret exceedingly that this Liberal government has been forced into the position of bringing in legislation such as has been introduced today. We know it had to be done. When we took over we found that in the Department of Finance the interest payments on the national debt had been increased by a million dollars a day. We found that the unemployment insurance fund was bankrupt. We found that the Department of National Health and Welfare was allowing the issuance of dangerous sample drugs to people free of charge. And now, in the Department of Labour, we find a situation which calls for legislation of a kind which many who sit on this side of the house find it onerous to support. But because we volunteered in 1962 and re-enlisted in 1963 in the army to clean up the Augean stables which, according to the Greek myth, stank so much that two rivers were needed to clean them out-because we volunteered to clean up that mess, we mean to do so right now.

It is well known that under the law of Canada the grounds for deporting a landed immigrant are, as they ought to be, much more stringent than those which apply to someone who is just a visitor. Yes, a serious change which I am sure the right hon. gentleman supported, because it was the kind of humanitarian thing he liked to associate himself with. Up until that time it had been the law of Canada that no one could be admitted to the country as an immigrant who had any criminal record. The law was changed to provide that if a man many years previously had a criminal record and if he appeared to be reformed he could, in certain circumstances, be admitted. This parliament made that change in the clear light of day. It was a very deliberate change and was made before I was a member of parliament, and it was in pursuance of that change in the law that the action was taken in 1954.
I have no doubt that, considering what has happened since then, if one had had the advantage of hindsight at that time, Mr. Banks would not have been landed. Maybe it was an error of judgment. That may well be, but I do say that it was in accordance with the law which I had no part in making. It was a decision made by my predecessor before I became the minister, but which, I have said before and I say again, I know he made conscientiously after the most careful examination of all the facts.
Whether it was wise or whether it was not wise is another matter, but anybody who suggests it was made by my predecessor on any other grounds than a conscientious desire to carry out the law made by parliament, does not know my predecessor in that office very well.

If at the second reading stage there were other alternatives, hon. members were free to place them in the form of amendments and test them in the opinion of the house. The house has now accepted the principle of the bill and is considering it in committee.
Several hon. gentlemen have asked me why there are no provisions in this bill to deal with the shipping companies. Mr. Justice Norris, as hon. gentlemen know, spent about a year studying the matter and preparing a report. I believe he reviewed this situation completely. It is true that he did apply some strictures to the shipping companies, especially the Canada Steamship Lines; but in his recommendations he made no proposals to the

Minister of Labour in respect of action to be taken against the shipping companies. He made a proposal that we ought to set up a government trusteeship. I presume he had concluded, on the basis of the evidence, that the root problem in the situation, notwithstanding the evidence of collusion that he found, rested within the S.I.U., and if that root problem were solved the rest of the situation would adjust itself. This is the only conclusion I can draw from this recommendation.
I say further to hon. members of the committee that if parliament approves this measure and if, as we expect, capable and reputable trustees are appointed to administer the trusteeship, they will be able to root out any future collusion that may exist, or conspiracy on the part of the shipping companies. The report of the inquiry was to the Minister of Labour and, in this bill, I am acting upon the recommendations of the commissioner in respect of the maritime transportation unions.
Now, with respect to any further actions that hon. members may feel are necessary or justified in so far as the shipping companies are concerned, that is a matter for the government as a whole. It would be a matter of government policy with which I cannot deal in a committee studying a bill whose principle has been approved by the House of Commons.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Before the minister answers,
I should like to ask two short questions somewhat related to the question asked by the hon. member for Timiskaming. Why are there two descriptions of property, one under the word "property", and one under the

Maritime Transportation Unions words "property of a maritime union"? Would the minister explain why there are these two descriptions of property in this bill? Also, not being a lawyer, would he explain for my benefit, or illustrate what is meant by "corporeal or incorporeal" property?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, may I be allowed to answer the last question first, with the leave of the Minister of Labour and more particularly of the chairman of the committee. The reason why in paragraph (d) of clause 2 the word "property" is defined is to make sure that, in whoever's hands it be found, the whole concept of property, whenever necessary for the carrying out of the purposes of the unions, is provided for under the act. In paragraph (e) that property which is defined in paragraph (d) may be in the hands of two types of unions, those which are incorporated and which can hold their own personal property-they are provided for in subparagraph (ii) of paragraph (e)- and those unions who are not incorporated and may not hold property themselves, but whose property is in the hands of other persons, in the hands of their administrators. Those are the type of unions provided for in paragraph (e)(ii).
As to the first question put regarding the generality of the definition of the word "property", the hon. member may rest assured that this is a matter which has been the cause of serious concern to, and therefore serious consideration by, the government. We came to the conclusion very sincerely that if there is to be a trusteeship the application of this legislation and the fulfilment of its purpose becomes impossible if the funds and investments of the union are not at the disposal of the trustees.
Second, I think one will agree that if the trustees are not vested with the control of the moneys of these unions the whole purpose of the bill may be defeated by anybody seizing control in a fashion not in conformity with the purposes of this legislation. The question is very serious and I think we all thank the hon. member for raising it. However, he will notice that, for instance in clause 11 (2), the government has shown its intention not to vest the trustees with these moneys just for the purpose of doing so. Because in the case of moneys which are directed to the establishment of a welfare plan for the seamen, the paragraph vesting the trustees with these moneys does not apply if the moneys are administered by trust companies or insurance companies. I think this explains the situation and I hope it answers the question.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a question with regard to clause 2 (c), which defines a maritime transportation union and a
[Mr. Herridge.}
maritime union, as those terms are used in the bill. subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: I think that if my friend would refer to the recommendations of the Norris report he would find that Mr. Justice Norris pointed out the possibility of the extension of the operations of such combinations along the seaway in Canadian and United States ports, and on the coast of Canada. The trusteeship might be very ineffective if responsibility was assigned to the trustees for one particular area and difficulties arose elsewhere which frustrated the operation of the trusteeship. That is why the total field is covered.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Naturally, Mr. Chairman, the minister would not want to name whom he intends to appoint to the board of trustees, but there is one recommendation of Mr. Justice Norris with which I do not agree, and

it is an important point. He suggested that the board should be made up of a chairman with wide legal experience, an economist with some knowledge of labour matters, and some person experienced in transportation. Does he plan to have a lawyer, an economist, or what type of person is he thinking of appointing? I do not care how good an economist may be, how experienced a person may be in the transportation field, or whether you have a first class legal mind. Unless somebody knows how trade unions work and can lead these people step by step into assuming responsibility, I think the trusteeship is likely to break down because of a lack of understanding and communication between the board of trustees and the unions they are supposed to be supervising. subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES

I agree that it is necessary to have on the trusteeship body a person very knowledgeable in labour matters, preferably someone with personal experience of the conduct of union affairs. With these two considerations in mind we shall attempt to get an effective group of men to discharge this responsibility. I am in full agreement with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that the trade union aspect ought definitely to be represented.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: I note that the entire cost of the trusteeship is to be borne, as I understand it, by the government of Canada and thus, ultimately, by the taxpayers of this country. subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: I think it would be reasonable to expect the taxpayers to assume the cost of these proceedings because this is to be a public trusteeship-the trustees are to be appointed by the government pursuant to an act of this parliament. If a private trusteeship had been in effect, and if the prime responsibility rested upon the union movement, I think it would be fair for the unions themselves to have borne the expense, and this is what was in mind in the now lamented private memorandum we had worked on. In this case, however, the trusteeship is public, not private and it seems reasonable to me that we should deal with it as an expense to the taxpayers.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 6 agreed to.

Maritime Transportation Unions
On clause 7-Function of the trustees.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
I feel this is one of the more important clauses of the bill since it outlines the responsibilities and duties of the trustees. It tells them, in fact, how they are to operate and what powers they are to receive. With reference to clause 7 (1), the question has arisen in the minds of some of us whether or not, according to this wording, the trustees will be subject to and have to operate within the ordinary terms of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. I, for one, feel that the legislation as drafted does not make this point clear. It says nothing about it one way or another. It does say specifically in line three that the trustees must act in accordance with the legislation which we now have under consideration, but I am wondering whether any thought has been given to the point which I have raised.
It has occurred to me that if, immediately following the words "this Act" in line three, words to this effect were added-"and subject to the terms of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigations Act" the position would be made entirely clear. At the back of this suggestion is my idea that these trustees should in effect be acting as if they were the duly elected officers of the trade unions involved, and that it should be clearly set out that they would be expected to deal with such matters as negotiations with the companies when the time comes for these negotiations to be carried out. In other words, they would be acting as if they were officers of a trade union dealing with the companies and subject to the normal operation of our labour laws. Has the minister any comment to make on that suggestion?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: It is intended that the trustees should fully observe the normal industrial relations law, and there is nothing in this bill which would supersede the application of the act to which the hon. member has referred. We fully expect that the trustees will operate within that framework.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
With respect to clause 7(5) I see that there is a power of delegation so extensive that it would amount to a complete abnegation, if it were exercised, of the responsibilities of the trustees. Under the subsection the trustees may delegate "any or all of the duties and powers of the trustees to any person appointed by the trustees." As I read this, the trustees could delegate all the powers which this legislation gives them to a single person or to a group of persons. The danger which I see is the possibility of the trustees delegating the whole


of the powers to any one individual. I am wondering what is the purpose behind this subclause?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
I think we have to assume the trustees will delegate in accordance with the authority they will have under this bill. It may well be necessary to have this kind of delegation because of the extent of the operations coming under the trusteeship.
The Canadian maritime union has one local with 500 members. The S.I.U. has 17,000 members, with two divisions. The marine engineers have seven locals and the Canadian merchant service guild has two divisions with more than 2,400 members. The C.B.R.T. has 13 locals in various parts of the country, in the east and the west, so that it certainly will be necessary for the trustees to have this power of delegation, and presumably in certain instances this will not present any difficulty. Presumably there are certain unions which will operate normally without delegated powers, and the trustees will not have to probe very deeply into some of these operations where the unions are currently operated democratically.
It seems to me, while these powers are necessary, the possibility of delegation strengthens the capacity, even under trusteeship, for the locals to operate on their own.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Yukon has raised a good point. The delegation of powers by the board of trustees to elected officers of a union is perfectly understandable, and I recognize the delegation of powers to another person may be necessary because of the scattered nature of the operations. But this parliament is giving very wide powers to the board. The board in turn is going to have the authority to delegate these very wide powers to some other person, and if that person uses them in an irresponsible manner, then the board of trustees will be in trouble and we will be in trouble.
The kind of persons to whom these powers are delegated is an important matter. I think it comes back again to the whole question of the board of trustees. We have the minister's assurance that it is not going to be a board which meets once a month, and then the members carry on their regular occupations and leave a group of people to whom they delegate authority to discharge their responsibilities. The board must be full time, and must stay on the job. In addition, the people they select to whom they delegate responsibility on both coasts and at various points in Canada, will have to be carefully selected.
When the minister talks about selecting some person who has judicial experience there is something to be said for that, because a person with judicial experience is accepted

as being fairly objective and unbiased; but the fact remains, no matter how unbiased he may be we are all creatures of our own environments. Some judges have had most of their training in corporation law, and have spent most of their professional lives acting on behalf of corporations. They have that particular viewpoint; but there are judges-I could name two or three-who have had a good background in dealing with labour matters and who have acted frequently in labour cases, in conciliation and arbitration cases. When the minister is making the appointments I hope he will keep this in mind.
I feel that some person in the judiciary who has had a good association with labour, a good understanding of labour law and the principles involved in operating a union, ought to be selected. If that kind of person is not selected and the board delegates these responsibilities to some person who may have no understanding of trade union procedure, then there will be a complete breakdown in relations between the board and its appointees on the one hand, and the men who work the ships on the other.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: I agree with the comments of the hon. member that it ought to be the objective to select a person-even if that person is a member of the judiciary-with experience in labour matters. We shall make our effort in that direction.

speechtext: There is a question I was going to ask under clause 9, but in view of the fact the minister has directed his attention to subsection 5 of clause 7 I may as well ask it now. Is it intended that the exemption from individual liability envisaged under clause 9, so far as the trustees are concerned, will extend to those to whom the trustees have delegated power?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: I think the answer to this is that the trustees will not be a body corporate. Were they to constitute a body corporate then they would be placed in the same situation as directors or presidents of a company. It is only out of fairness to the trustees that the clause has been devised that way, and I think it must be read that the trustees, for all practical and legal purposes, will have the same type of responsibility with respect to funds, their application or otherwise, as the directors of a corporation personally would have in the same situation.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
What I wanted to take from that is the fact that that exemption from liability does not extend to people to whom the trustees might delegate authority under subclause 5. I want to know was this the
Maritime Transportation Unions intention, that such exemption from responsibility will not attach to those to whom powers are delegated under clause 7(5)?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: I have no authority to speak here, otherwise than in my own name, so far as my opinion of the text is concerned, but it is my clear opinion that this clause relieves only the trustees themselves, and in no way whoever may assume delegated authority from their hands.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: The minister's opinion is very helpful, but I think what my hon. friend and I are interested in is knowing whether it is the intention of the government that those to whom powers are delegated will not receive the same protection as the trustees under clause 9?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: I am advised by the Minister of Labour it is the intention that the clause be applied as the hon. member just suggested, so as not to free those exercising delegated power.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: I want to direct a question to the minister with regard to subclause 2(a). It provides for the establishment of advisory councils of seamen and their representatives and joint advisory councils of seamen and ship owners to advise, and so on. Could we have some explanation as to what the ship owners are going to be doing, and how it is envisaged they will fit into the general pattern of the trusteeship? We are somewhat mystified by it. I wonder whether the minister could elaborate on the role that it is intended the ship owners will play.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend will notice that Mr. Justice Norris did recommend the usefulness of having advisory committees of seamen on the one hand and of ship owners on the other. I think first of all it must be mentioned that the trustees will be free to decide on this point. They are free to appoint them or set them up if necessary. We think there is some value in the trustees having the opportunity to set up advisory committees of seamen on the one hand and to set up as well, if they so desire, a committee of ship management and labour. Surely it is common practice for labour and management to sit down together, and this may be a helpful development in this situation.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we are quite familiar with the idea of labour-management committees and labour-management co-operation, but it is not the usual thing for the leadership of a trade union to have the authority and responsibility to appoint an advisory council consisting of both its own people and management people. It seems to us
28902-5-223

Maritime Transportation Unions that this clause overlooks the fact that what is being appointed by this legislation is a board of trustees to administer the union. In our view these trustees are for the time being the heads of the union organization. Their purpose is to get things cleaned up and to get democratic processes operating again. But it appears to us that there is a suggestion here that there is to be a relationship on the part of these trustees with the management side that is not the usual thing in trade union organizations.
We feel that this same situation occurs in clause 7 (2) (c) where the trustees are given the right to tender advice to bargaining committees of a maritime union. If you couple with that the fact that the trustees may have an advisory council consisting of both labour and management, one wonders what kind of advice these trustees may give to a bargaining committee that is engaged in collective bargaining with management.
Our whole point is that if we accept the principle of trustees to run these unions for whatever period of time this legislation is in effect, they should in effect have the trade union point of view. It should be a clean, democratic, free trade union point of view; but nevertheless it should be the trade union point of view, and it is our feeling that point of view is set aside by the language both in 2 (a) and 2 (c).
For example, what happens if under 2 (c), -and I think 2 (a) and 2 (c) are related,- the committees that are doing the collective bargaining get advice from the trustees based on advice they have got from this joint advisory council, which is advice that suggests that the union seek less than it may be seeking in its collective bargaining? Does this not destroy the normal rights and privileges of a trade union? Should not the whole relationship between the trustees and management be just as much at arm's length so far as management is concerned as it is in the case of ordinary trade union officers?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: Before the minister answers I wonder whether I might ask a related question arising out of paragraph (c). To follow one step farther than the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has gone, I would point out that the trustees may delegate the power to enter into a collective bargaining agreement. If such a collective agreement is not effected, do the trustees have the power to call a legal strike under this legislation?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
The answer to the question is yes. May I point out to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that these councils are joint councils and they were made joint councils for the very reason that the


hon. member suggests. As I recollect, the Norris commission recommended a separate advisory body of employers or ship owners and we thought that we ought to protect the points made by my hon. friend, namely, that if in the management of a union the point of view of the ship owner was to be received at any stage it should be received in a meeting at which labour men were also represented. So there is that control in so far as the exercise of advice is concerned. It is control by the presence on that council of the seamen or representatives of the seamen.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: The minister does not seem to have got our point. What we are setting up here is not a body that has oversight of the relations between labour and management. What we are setting up here is a substitute for the trade union leadership itself. These trustees will take the place of the normal administrators of the trade unions concerned. Does the minister know of any trade union in this country where the officers of the trade union have the right, on their own initiative and authority, to set up a joint advisory council of labour and management, where the officers of the trade union name the representatives from the management side? It seems to us that our point is being missed by the minister.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: I think I see the point that the hon. gentleman makes. I take it that the hon. gentleman means that the trustees, as in the case of a trade union itself, ought not to be given the power, which a trade union would not otherwise have, to designate and appoint members for management on any joint advisory body.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: Any more than management should name the representatives of the union.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
I think the problem might be solved if instead of giving direct power to the trustees to establish advisory boards we gave them the power to promote the establishment of such boards. Then there would be no question of their having the right to appoint members from management or members from the union side. This would permit entire freedom of discussion and would, I think, place the trustees in the same situation as that in which a union would be in a case where a union would seek to convince management to get together with the union to try to form a joint committee. Therefore I would be ready to move an amendment myself, with the concurrence of the minister, who would agree, replacing the word "establish" by the words "promote the establishment of". Would that be agreeable to the

hon. gentleman? Then there would be no direct power given to them.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: I think the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration has caught our point and I believe the suggested change of wording may meet it, although we may have to look at it closely. The trustees may promote this sort of thing, but they are not given the power to name representatives of management. In other words, what we are trying to avoid here is company unionism in reverse.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: Perhaps we could proceed with the other clauses, Mr. Chairman, and come back to this subclause. In the meantime we could work out an amendment.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: On that point, Mr. Chairman, and following up the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I think what we must ensure is that the trusteeship which is to be set up here is in no way associated with management and should not be associated with management unless they are negotiating or renegotiating a general agreement. We take it for granted that union representation will be available to the trustees, and therefore the trustees will also be associated with management when the union feels they must meet the company to discuss a grievance. I was hoping he would reduce it to 1964, but having heard the amendment I think that the device of proclamation could be used at the end of one year just as easily as it could at the end of three or two years. I think the period is still too long and I suggest it be further reduced to December 31, 1964.
As the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings has just suggested to me, the act can always be extended by a separate act of parliament, and this amendment is a very complicated way of accomplishing the desired objective of making the extension subject to the review of the House of Commons. All the minister has to do is introduce another bill saying this one will be extended for whatever period the government feels necessary.

speechtext: I am told there is some difficulty in this connection. Although I believe the translators are working all night, I am not sure that this report will be available for Monday.
